results.title: Geopolitics
highlights: The logic of alliances in 1914, which led to World War I, has a modern-day parallel. The new Middle East alliance, of which NATO member Türkiye is a part, could drag Europe into regional conflicts, warns the EU-Expert. in 1950 (India) and 1949 (China), it was primarily the Soviet Union and later Russia that sought to achieve a policy of détente between the two countries. There are still trilateral relations between the countries today. For example, in the fight against Covid-19. However, there are several points of contention between China and India. Firstly, there are unresolved border issues. A dispute that has been raging since 1962. Since then, China has also supported Pakistan politically and economically. In 2020, the dispute escalated again when a brawl broke out between soldiers from China and India in the Indian district of Ladakh. According to the Indian military, twenty Indian soldiers are said to have been killed. The second major point of contention between China and India is the water supply. India draws a lot of its drinking water from the Brahmaputra, which has its source in the Himalayas. However, this is on Chinese territory. China diverted a lot of water to Beijing, which led to water shortages in Bangladesh and India. In principle, the Chinese Communist Party is striving to curb India's political influence in order to strengthen its own. Geopolitics: China as a military power China's geopolitical rise also has a lot to do with the People's Republic's massive defense spending. With 2.3 million soldiers, China has the largest army in the world. According to its own figures, the Chinese military owns 6,300 tanks, 350 warships, 49 aircraft carriers and 50 submarines. Although the number of soldiers has been reduced in recent years, spending has increased. The background to this is the planned modernization of equipment. China spent around EUR 174 billion on the military in 2019. However, experts suspect that much of this expenditure was spent on non-military items and cannot be clearly allocated. China's military budget for 2019 is therefore estimated at USD 261 billion. China wants to take on the same geopolitical role that the USA currently has. The army is to be deployed wherever a military presence is needed. Also to defend the security of its own country and Chinese interests. Indo-Pacific conflict China is embroiled in various territorial disputes in the Indo-Pacific, some of which have been simmering for decades. The People's Republic is therefore massively expanding its navy and claims several islands for itself, particularly in the South China Sea. In order to better protect itself from China's claims to power, Australia has agreed an Indo-Pacific pact with the USA and the UK. Among other things, this involves the delivery of nuclear-powered submarines. However, Nils Schmid, the foreign policy spokesperson for the SPD parliamentary group in the Bundestag, emphasizes that this would not just be a contract on armaments, but a strategic cooperation. Originally, France and the EU were to take on the role of the USA, but Australia terminated the contract to supply the submarines. Schmid insists that Europe must consider a strategy to ensure that it does not give up its own influence in the Indo-Pacific. After all, trade is always embedded in geopolitical considerations. What is the relationship between Germany and China like? Relations between Germany and China are complicated. On the one hand, economic cooperation is important for both sides. The volume of trade amounted to EUR 212.1 billion in 2020. Germany imported more (EUR 116.3 billion) than it exported (EUR 95.9 billion). But there are major points of contention. One of them is the human rights situation in the People's Republic. Another is that Germany believes it is not an equal trading partner. In March 2019, the EU Commission even called China a "systemic rival" and even imposed sanctions on the People's Republic. The greatest common ground is political cooperation on environmental protection. The People's Republic wants to be CO₂-neutral by 2060. Federal Environment Minister Svenja Schulze signed an agreement to this effect with her counterpart Huang Runqui. Points of contention between Germany and China The human rights situation in China repeatedly leads to criticism of the People's Republic in Germany. In Xinjian, Uyghur minorities are persecuted and sent to re-education camps. German companies also benefit from their forced labor. In addition, there is the suppression of the democracy movement in Hong Kong and threatening military gestures towards Taiwan. An open dispute then flared up between Germany and China over the "Second Law on Enhancing the Security of Information Technology Systems". Its requirements for participation in the expansion of the 5G network in Germany make market access extremely difficult for Huawei. What is the relationship between the USA and China like? The political atmosphere between the USA and China is extremely tense. Following the election of Joe Biden as the new US president, the country has continued its hard line against the People's Republic. The confrontational course serves to "protect core US national security interests and democratic values", writes the White House in a statement. The background to this is Biden's measure to blacklist 59 Chinese companies. Observers are of the opinion that US policy towards China is primarily intended to prevent the People's Republic from becoming a world power and technology leader in key technologies. To this end, US President Joe Biden, like his predecessor Donald Trump, is relying on the principle of decoupling. This is based on an "unbundling" of the American and Chinese economies. Because imports and exports are to be reduced, both countries are seeking new partnerships and trade agreements. What does dual circulation mean? China's dual circulation policy is intended to strengthen the domestic economy. The principle of dual circulation is a central component of the current five-year plan, which was adopted in 2021. Dual circulation is intended to make the People's Republic less dependent on imports. This is to be achieved by introducing subsidies for domestic companies and import barriers for non-Chinese companies. In addition to the trade war with the USA, the coronavirus pandemic has also fueled the dual circulation policy. China does not want to be dependent on global trading partners for its growth plans. The People's Republic also expects the dual-circulation policy to give new impetus to its Made in China 2025 strategy, which aims to grow the country into the world's leading high-tech power. China's Silk Road: geopolitics through loans Around 140 countries are part of China's New Silk Road project. Also known as One Belt, One Road or the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). This is a collection of various infrastructure measures to improve global trade flows. The People's Republic has been pushing ahead with the plans since 2013. The aim is to bring the resource-rich countries in Africa closer to China in particular. However, 18 of the 27 European member states have also signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). This is a declaration of intent to integrate into the New Silk Road. The New Silk Road projects are financed by banks and funds that provide loans to the participating countries. However, the collateralization of the loans by China is extremely strict. In the event of a bankruptcy, the Chinese loans must be serviced as a priority. However, because the contracts are secret, other lenders are unaware of the debtor's financial situation. They are correspondingly cautious. China is using the loans to pursue its geopolitical interests. results.title: Taiwan coast guard forces four China coast guard ships out of Kinmen restricted waters | Taiwan Defence
highlights: Taiwan coast guard forces four China coast guard ships out of Kinmen restricted waters | Taiwan Defence Taiwan's coast guard forced four China coast guard ships out of Kinmen restricted waters after a two-hour grey-zone probe. Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration said four China Coast Guard ships entered Kinmen's restricted waters on Tuesday morning, 13 October 2026, and left only after Taiwanese patrol boats shadowed them one-to-one, broadcast warnings in Mandarin and English, and used close-range blocking to stop them pushing deeper toward the island group. According to a statement from the Coast Guard's Kinmen-Matsu-Penghu Branch, the Twelfth Patrol District detected the Chinese vessels around 8 a.m. Taipei time as they approached the outer edge of Kinmen's restricted waters. The hull numbers listed were 14608, 14531, 14607 and 14529. Coast Guard cutters were ordered forward to the boundary line before the Chinese ships crossed it. At 8.52 a.m., the four China Coast Guard ships entered Kinmen restricted waters from south of Lieyu, also known as Little Kinmen, sailing in a single-column formation. Taiwanese patrol boats matched each Chinese vessel one-to-one, collected evidence throughout the transit, and used radio broadcasts plus near-range deterrence to keep the formation from pressing farther into the controlled zone. The branch said all four Chinese coast guard ships left Kinmen waters at 11.08 a.m. The transit therefore lasted a little over two hours from entry to exit under continuous Taiwanese escort and warning. Coast Guard officials characterised the sailing pattern as fake law enforcement and real power expansion, arguing that the manoeuvre seeks to change the local maritime status quo and threatens navigation safety and order around Kinmen. The service urged China's coast guard to stop harassment that could raise tensions or spark a clash, and said it would keep cutters on round-the-clock watch to defend Taiwan's sovereignty and maritime security. Kinmen sits only a short distance from the Chinese city of Xiamen, which makes even brief China Coast Guard entries into Taiwan's declared restricted waters a high-visibility grey-zone test for Taiwan's coast guard and, behind it, the wider defence posture that treats the outlying islands as an early-warning front against Chinese maritime pressure. Central News Agency, TaiSounds and SETN all carried the same Kinmen-Matsu-Penghu Branch account of the Tuesday intrusion, including the four hull numbers, the Lieyu approach, the one-to-one escort tactic and the 11.08 a.m. exit. The reporting frames the episode as a post-National Day return to routine China Coast Guard probing around Taiwan's frontline islands rather than a one-off holiday-week stunt. For Taiwan's military and coast guard planners, the operational lesson is continuity: Chinese coast guard hulls that show up in column south of Lieyu still have to be met ship-for-ship, recorded, warned and turned around without letting the encounter escalate into a boarding or collision crisis that Beijing could spin as Taiwanese overreaction.

results.title: Blink and You’ll Miss Trump’s Quiet Defiance of China - Newsweek
highlights: A rumor is circulating that President Donald Trump has caved to China’s most important demand: Taiwan. It’s been fueled by the usual tendency to listen to what the Republican says rather than what he does. Trump was one of the first U.S. presidents to publicly admit that attempting to defend Taiwan from a Chinese attack might be folly. The democratically governed island is only 80 miles from the Chinese coast, with outlying territory even closer. Defense planners in Washington and Taipei must confront an inconvenient truth, but the obstacle tells us little about American resolve in the next Taiwan Strait crisis. It also ignores the challenges Beijing faces, regardless of the U.S. appetite to fight another war. Even the most skeptical of leaders in the White House would find it hard to reverse decades of U.S. policy designed to preserve American interests in Taiwan, both strategic and economic. A closer look at the Trump administration’s recent actions suggests his words and actions don’t match—and not in a way that would please China. Trump’s eagerness to make up with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping led to a much-publicized state visit to Beijing in May that was full of pomp and circumstance. He returned the favor last month in an unprecedented welcome for America’s top geopolitical rival. Trump knows how much Xi wants Taiwan—control of the high-tech island would be a legacy-defining win for any Communist Party leader—so policy analysts in Washington, D.C., balked at his apparent openness to discussing current and future arms sales to Taipei with Beijing—the very thing keeping the Chinese military at bay. China’s state media outlets rejoiced at what they saw as a return to realism: the U.S. president, who seemed more preoccupied with the Western Hemisphere and issues at the United States' southern border, was finally coming to terms with the growing cross-strait power imbalance tilting in Beijing’s favor. He was saying all the right things. Xi will be disappointed this month by reports that the Department of Defense is preparing to place U.S. officials at the heart of Taiwan’s military establishment to cooperate more closely on joint planning and help Taipei integrate its new American weapons systems with the Taiwanese armed forces. The move is part of a $14.77 million multiyear program led by Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy. It elevates U.S.-Taiwan defense ties to a level not seen since the two governments shared a mutual defense pact from 1955-1979, only terminated when Washington and Beijing established formal diplomatic ties. It was always an open secret that the U.S. dispatches hundreds of military instructors to assist Taiwan each year. The new program institutionalizes the quiet security cooperation. In early October, two F-16 fighter jets landed at an air base in eastern Taiwan to supplement its outnumbered air force. They were part of an $8 billion order for 66 aircraft first approved by Trump back in 2019, adding to 150 older variants purchased in the 1990s. The delivery, set to be completed in the next two years, was so significant that it drew a critical response from North Korea, a Chinese ally, which warned via state media that the United States was destabilizing the region. This month, Taiwanese newspapers also reported the anticipated delivery of 128 Harpoon anti-ship missiles and 500 Stinger air defense missiles later this year, along with various munitions and aircraft maintenance contracts critical to sustaining Taiwan’s fighting power. Elsewhere in the region, the U.S. is pressing ahead with joint training exercises with security ally Japan to prepare for a potential conflict with China, including by deploying NMESIS anti-ship missile launchers to the far-western Japanese island of Yonaguni, around 70 miles off Taiwan’s east coast, according to plans published by the town government. At home, the FBI embarrassed Beijing by publicizing the arrest of a U.S. citizen who allegedly surveilled the Seattle-based son of Taiwan’s sitting president on behalf of China’s main spy agency, the Ministry of State Security. China denied any knowledge of the And despite concerns about what last month’s Trump-Xi summit would mean for U.S. commitments to Taiwan, the meeting produced little of note on the island. The Chinese government said Xi warned Trump that his handling of Taiwan would affect relations between the two countries, but Trump said the leaders hardly discussed the issue. “We didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan. He understands very much how I feel,” Trump said. China cares a lot more about what America’s leaders do than what they say. In December, after the Trump administration announced a record $11.1 billion arms package for Taiwan that included dozens of HIMARS rocket launchers and hundreds of ATACMS missile systems, the Chinese military described the U.S.’s decision as “extremely irresponsible, extremely dangerous and extremely harmful.” Despite multiple attempts to get Trump to build on a 1982 U.S.-China joint communiqué that promised to gradually reduce arms sales to Taiwan, the president has yet to budge, only deepening Beijing’s mistrust of U.S. words. That’s just as well; China wasn’t planning on slowing down anyway. Colby, the Pentagon policy chief overseeing the placement of U.S. personnel in Taiwan’s Defense Ministry, recognizes Beijing’s broader designs after Taiwan. His book, *The Strategy of Denial*, describes a Chinese state that intends to use the occupation of Taiwan as a stepping stone to project power across the Pacific at America’s expense. The new F-16s delivered to Taiwan this month arrived after years of delays, partly due to supply chain disruptions and the relocation of Lockheed Martin’s factory. While China is already testing sixth-generation fighter jets, Taiwan will have to wait longer to see its F-16 order fulfilled. They are part of a $29.72 billion arms backlog that has remained largely stagnant for years across multiple administrations, according to a tracker built by the Taiwan Security Monitor group at George Mason University in Virginia. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month that the delivery of arms to Taiwan had been delayed by factors including U.S. industrial capacity and the ongoing Iran war, which has expended large numbers of munitions like the Patriot interceptor—also high on Taipei’s order list. Trump’s biggest test, however, is a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan that has been sitting on his desk since late last year. Xi and his officials have told their American counterparts in no uncertain terms that the deal could seriously damage the recent detente between the two governments, but any wavering on Trump’s part will be endless ammunition for his Democratic opponents. Beijing is holding future leaders’ meetings and potential trade deals as collateral, and the White House knows that green-lighting another record sale would kill any chance of Trump meeting Xi at APEC in November and at the G20 a month later. He needs both to secure more American access to the Chinese market. Rubio said the deal won’t be canceled, but it could be split up or watered down so Trump can keep up appearances. David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said on X this month that Trump “is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody.” We probably wouldn't go that far, but Trump’s actions haven’t come close to bringing the type of doom many have feared.

She added that the foreign officials had visited Taiwan and received visits by “Taiwan independence separatists,” as well as “spread disinformation about Chinese cyberattacks to smear and attack China, creating a seriously negative international impact.” Paraguay and Belize are among the last 12 remaining diplomatic allies of Taiwan, an island democracy China sees as its own territory, to be annexed by force if necessary. In recent years, Beijing has increased its military pressure on the island, sending warplanes and military ships near it almost daily. It has also ramped up a campaign of winning over its diplomatic partners. Countries including Nauru, Honduras and Nicaragua have switched allegiances from Taiwan to Beijing in recent years. Taipei’s remaining diplomatic allies are mostly smaller countries in Central America, the Caribbean and South Pacific, along with Eswatini in southern Africa and Vatican City. The sanctions against Villate and Fonseca are mostly symbolic, as officials from countries that have ties with Taiwan do not generally travel to China. The curbs include freezing any assets the officials might have in China; denial of visas and entry into China; prohibiting any Chinese individuals and organizations from cooperating with them. The governments of Belize and Paraguay did not immediately react to In July, Paraguay and the US Embassy in its capital, Asunción, said cybersecurity attacks linked to the Chinese government had compromised Paraguay's state systems. China vehemently denied the accusations. The US State Department condemned China's sanctions on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere for exercising their sovereign rights,” department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said. Taiwanese Premier Cho Jung-tai on Tuesday told reporters that the island democracy is a sovereign country and that China has no right to interfere in its internal affairs or influence its foreign relations. He said Taiwan would continue working with its allies and other democracies to uphold freedom and democracy, maintain regional peace and security, and resist “any expansion of hegemonic or authoritarian forces.” China and Taiwan have been governed separately since 1949, when a civil war brought the Communist Party to power in Beijing. Defeated Nationalist Party forces fled to Taiwan. The island has operated with its own government since then. Taiwan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi also criticized China’s moves, noting that Taiwan’s international visibility is growing. “Are they going to sanction the entire world?” he said.

results.title: Lai Spoke of Freedom. Beijing Answered With Live Fire. Deterrence Comes First.
highlights: Days after President Lai Ching-te's National Day address, China declared live-fire zones in five sea areas along its coast. Taipei is watching closely. Washington should keep strength, not hope, at the center of its China policy. On Saturday, Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te used his National Day address to say Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom. By Sunday, provincial authorities across China were closing off sea zones for new live-fire drills. China's Maritime Safety Administration announced no-sail notices for five areas running from the South China Sea up to the northeastern province of Liaoning, as Reuters reported in a story carried by the Taipei Times. The closest zone to Taiwan lies off Zhejiang province. None sits directly around the island itself. Radio Taiwan International reported the drills span the Bohai Sea, Yellow Sea, East China Sea, South China Sea, and other waters, and are scheduled to run five days. Taiwan's Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo told reporters the preliminary assessment is that the activity involves coastal and air-defense artillery firing drills, with limited impact on the waters around Taiwan. He did not stop there. "We adhere to the principle of 'anticipating the enemy as broadly as possible,'" Koo said, "so we will continue to closely monitor their activities, whether firing or military training." He added that China's repeated drills aimed at stirring tension in the Indo-Pacific warrant close scrutiny and condemnation. Beijing has not formally tied this week's drills to Lai's speech. It did not need to. On Sunday, China's Ministry of National Defense accused Lai of exaggerating the threat from China and trying to "seek independence through force." It called the People's Liberation Army's training around Taiwan "entirely justified." Su Tzu-yun of Taiwan's Institute for National Defense and Security Research told TaiwanPlus that Beijing first released a CCTV video signaling its resolve on "national unity," then announced the drills across multiple seas. "This serves as a political statement," he said. The timeline tells the story. China has not held full war games around Taiwan since late December, when it staged them in response to an $11 billion U.S. arms sale, the largest ever. Last week, the State Department called China's maritime actions off Taiwan's east coast "deeply destabilizing," after Reuters reported the first known sighting of a Chinese maritime militia boat in those waters in August. Beijing's foreign ministry answered that the waters belong to China and its conduct there is "beyond reproach." Washington's response so far is the right one. TaiwanPlus reported that the State Department on Sunday praised Lai's speech for seeking to maintain stability in the region, after several statements from U.S. officials that ties with Taipei remain unchanged. Steady words matter. Steady hardware matters more. Col. Rob Maness (ret.) argued in his October 12 column that Beijing tests American resolve constantly and moves only when it judges aggression to be cheap. His conclusion: deterrence has to come before everything else in the Pacific. This week's drills are one more data point. Every no-sail zone and every artillery barrage is rehearsal and message at the same time. It is tempting to call these exercises routine and best ignored. Routine is the point. Beijing wants the world numb to live fire off its coast so that the next exercise, closer and larger, draws a shrug. Taipei's defense minister is not shrugging. Washington should not either. Peace through strength comes down to a few concrete steps. U.S. and allied forces in the Western Pacific stay ready. Taiwan's air defense and ammunition deliveries stay on schedule. Keep Japan, the Philippines, and Australia close. Answer intimidation with capability, not with silence. Lai said Taiwan will not give up its freedom. Beijing answered with artillery. America's answer should be readiness.

results.title: Will the Trump–Xi Bargain Divide Asia? - Argument - Eagle Intelligence Reports
highlights: When Xi left Washington, his first state visit in more than a decade had produced no breakthrough. The two governments extended a trade truce by two months, established an AI incident channel, and agreed to accelerate work on military crisis communications. More consequential, though, was a small amendment to their shared formula. In Beijing in May, the two leaders had agreed to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on “fairness and reciprocity.” In Washington, “respect” was added, and Wang Yi promptly defined it as respect specifically for each side’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, social system, and “core interests and major concerns.” Because the phrase originated in Chinese strategic thinking and was adopted by American diplomats, critics in Washington have read it as a concession to Beijing. But authorship is not the central question. What matters is whether Washington and Beijing are beginning to construct a set of informal rules for a rivalry neither side expects to end any time soon. Neither government has abandoned policies the other regards as threatening. Washington still describes its forward military presence as the foundation of regional order, while Beijing treats Taiwan as a question of territorial integrity and pushes to limit American military support for the island. Xi’s “new type of major-country relations,” first floated during his visit to Washington as vice president in 2012 and made the centerpiece of his 2013 summit with Barack Obama at Sunnylands, rested on three principles: no conflict or confrontation, mutual respect, including for “core interests,” and win-win cooperation. Washington welcomed the first and distrusted the second, fearing that “mutual respect” would be read as deference to Chinese claims on Taiwan and in the East and South China Sea. Xi’s current definition sounds familiar. Cooperation is to remain the “mainstay,” competition is to stay “within proper limits,” and differences are to be managed. , however, changed more than the vocabulary. In 2013, Washington still hoped to accommodate a rising China within an order whose rules it had largely written. By 2026, each side holds instruments that can seriously damage the other. The United States has spent nearly a decade restricting Chinese access to advanced technology, and China showed during the tariff war of 2025 that its grip on rare-earth processing can disrupt American industry. The Busan truce of last October halted that escalation. A formula once meant to reassure a rising power is now being used by two powers that expect their competition to continue, even if Xi, on arriving in Washington, insisted that the two countries should be “partners The institutions chartered at the May 2026 summit in Beijing and put into operation in Washington show how such overlap might be organized. A Board of Trade manages trade in non-sensitive goods, while a Board of Investment provides a channel for investment-related disputes. In Washington, the Board of Trade agreed on recommendations for preferential tariffs covering $30 billion of non- sensitive trade in each direction. The two governments have also formalized a dialogue on advanced AI and opened a channel for AI-related incidents. Compartmentalization works only as long as a failure in one domain does not spill into the others, which is hardest to prevent where either side believes a fundamental interest is at stake. Given Taiwan’s central role in global semiconductor production, a crisis over the island could quickly expose the limits of this compartmentalization, turning commercial concessions and technology restrictions into instruments of coercion rather than mechanisms for stabilizing the relationship. In such circumstances, even agreements designed to insulate economic relations from strategic competition could become subordinate to military considerations. Beijing wants Taiwan treated as the central political question in the relationship, U.S. technology controls confined to a narrow security perimeter, and American alliances prevented from hardening into an integrated anti-China coalition. Washington, meanwhile, is asking China to live with an enduring U.S. military presence, refrain from coercion against Taiwan and U.S. allies, and accept targeted export controls as legitimate security policy. Taiwan shows how quickly that line can blur. In December 2025, the administration approved an $11 billion arms package for the island, the largest ever. A second package worth about $14 billion, including Patriot interceptors and NASAMS air defense missiles, was cleared by Congress in January 2026 and still requires the president’s approval. After his visit to Beijing, Trump said he was holding it “in abeyance,” that the decision “depends on China,” and that it was “a very good negotiating chip.” He also acknowledged discussing arms sales with Xi “in great detail.” A week later, the acting secretary of the Navy offered a second explanation, telling senators that the sale had been paused to conserve munitions for the war against Iran. The two explanations do not exclude each other, but only the first turns an arms sale into an object of negotiation with Beijing. Before the Washington summit, Beijing reportedly went further. According to Reuters, it had asked Washington to halt deliveries of weapons Taiwan had already ordered and was preparing to press its reading of the 1982 communiqué, in which the United States stated an intention to reduce arms sales over time. The Six Assurances of the same year, declassified only in 2020, record that Washington had not agreed to prior consultations with Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan. One conceivable basis for reciprocal restraint would require Washington not to support a unilateral declaration of Taiwanese independence and Beijing not to alter the status quo through force or coercion. Such an understanding could reduce the risk of war without settling sovereignty. Negotiating the timing or scope of an individual arms sale would not, by itself, grant Beijing a veto. But repeated concessions or an expectation of prior consultation could gradually normalize Chinese influence over decisions that belong to Washington and Taipei. A workable form of strategic stability would therefore have to rest on mutual restraint without mutual vetoes. The pending decision on the $14 billion package will offer an early indication of whether that distinction can hold. The next tests are close at hand. China hosts the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, the United States hosts the G20 later in the year, the trade truce expires in January 2027, and the Taiwan arms package still awaits a decision. Each will show what the two sides mean by “proper limits.” A less immediate but potentially more revealing test will be the succession of the Dalai Lama. He has vested sole authority to recognize his successor in the Gaden Phodrang Trust, while Beijing insists that any reincarnation must be approved under Chinese law. Because the trust and the Tibetan exile institutions are based in India, the dispute could test how far other governments are expected to accommodate Beijing’s definition of its “core interests.” Whether it becomes a matter of U.S.–China bargaining remains uncertain, but the underlying distinction is the same: recognition of a strategic concern is not equivalent to accepting authority over decisions made beyond China’s borders. If Washington and Beijing limit their own conduct, keep crisis channels open, and practice reciprocal restraint, they may make a dangerous rivalry more predictable without necessarily curtailing the sovereignty of smaller states. But bilateral calm purchased by giving either power a say over what third countries may do would divide Asia into informal spheres negotiated over the heads of Tokyo, Manila, Seoul, and Taipei.

results.title: Trump’s China Opening and Japan’s Taiwan Anxiety – The Diplomat
highlights: Trump’s China Opening and Japan’s Taiwan Anxiety Tokyo fears being sidelined again as Washington and Beijing recalibrate their relationship. Call it the “Trump Shock.” The apparent closeness between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at their recent Beijing summit – along with Trump’s deferential posture toward Xi – sent shockwaves through Tokyo. This may one day be remembered in Japan as the “Trump Shock.” For Japanese policymakers, the summit revived memories of the 1971 “Nixon Shock,” when Washington began the process of normalizing relations with Beijing and Japan learned of the rapprochement only after the fact. More than half a century later, Tokyo is once again anxiously watching the world’s two most powerful leaders redefine their relationship increasingly in G-2 terms – while Japan fears being sidelined once again. No modern Japanese leader has adopted a more explicitly pro-Taiwan or hawkish China posture than Takaichi. Echoing the late Abe Shinzo’s famous formulation that “a Taiwan contingency is a Japanese contingency,” she argued in the Diet last November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” under Japan’s security legislation. Relations deteriorated sharply in the months that followed. Beijing imposed economic countermeasures – reducing flights, suspending seafood imports, and tightening rare earth export controls – while cooling political exchanges with Tokyo. “It’s a little bit of a difference. But, you know, there’s a lot of support for Taiwan, from Japan and from countries from that area,” Trump said at the White House on May 11, referring to Tokyo’s increasingly robust support for Taipei, including Takaichi’s own remarks regarding a Taiwan contingency. At the same time, he downplayed the likelihood of a cross-strait conflict. Ahead of the summit, Trump also stated that he intended to discuss future U.S. arms sales to Taiwan with Xi. He later acknowledged the issue had been discussed “in great detail” during the talks — immediately triggering concern in both Taipei and Tokyo. Since 1982, the “Six Assurances” have underpinned Washington’s unofficial commitment to Taiwan, including a pledge not to consult Beijing in advance on arms sales to Taipei. Together with the Taiwan Relations Act, those assurances have underpinned decades of deterrence and strategic ambiguity in the Taiwan Strait. If Washington were to move even informally toward prior consultation with Beijing over Taiwan arms sales, many in Asia would interpret it as a significant shift in long-standing U.S. policy. Following the summit, Trump held only a brief phone call with Takaichi during his return flight from Beijing. Although both governments publicly described the exchange positively, it did little to calm concerns inside Tokyo that Japan may not have been fully consulted regarding the substance of the summit talks. For many in Japan, the call appeared less like close alliance coordination than an exercise in political damage control. Taiwan sits at the center of the First Island Chain – the arc stretching from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines that has long formed the strategic backbone of U.S. maritime presence in the Western Pacific. Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, Yonaguni, lies just over 100 kilometers from Taiwan. Were Taiwan to come under Beijing’s strategic orbit, China’s military reach would extend dramatically closer to Okinawa and Japan’s southwestern islands. Kadena Air Base would effectively sit on the front line of a transformed regional balance. Japan’s sea lanes, through which much of its energy imports flow, would also become substantially more exposed. There is a phrase that periodically resurfaces in Tokyo diplomatic circles: “Japan passing.” It refers to the recurring fear that Japan could be bypassed as Washington and Beijing negotiate the regional order over Tokyo’s head. Trump’s diplomatic style reinforces that anxiety. Unlike alliance-focused U.S. administrations of the postwar era, Trump has consistently emphasized bilateral dealmaking, personal diplomacy with authoritarian leaders, and transactional flexibility. From Tokyo’s perspective, that creates uncertainty about whether alliance coordination remains the organizing principle of U.S. Asia policy – or whether it has become merely one variable in a broader geopolitical bargain. Washington also has strong incentives to stabilize its relationship with Beijing. Simultaneous tensions involving Iran, Russia, global trade, and energy prices have increased pressure on the United States to avoid confrontation on multiple fronts. China, meanwhile, retains leverage through its relationships with both Moscow and Tehran, as well as through its central role in global supply chains. In that broader geopolitical context, Taiwan risks becoming part of a much larger strategic negotiation. The concern is not simply that the United States is engaging China. The deeper fear is that Japan could find itself strategically exposed after antagonizing Beijing – having hardened its Taiwan posture under the assumption of strong American backing, only to discover that Washington itself may now be pursuing a more pragmatic accommodation with Xi. Japan remains economically dependent on China and strategically dependent on the United States. Managing that dual dependence has always required careful diplomacy. It becomes far harder if Washington and Beijing seek a more stable relationship while Japan’s own ties with China continue deteriorating. For Takaichi personally, the stakes are especially high. results.title: How Taiwan Activates Beijing’s Chosen Fear
highlights: The standard explanations for why Taiwan is so important to the Chinese Communist Party are familiar: territorial integrity, credibility of deterrence commitments, great power competition with the United States, the strategic value of the first island chain, and the semiconductor industry concentrated in TSMC’s fabrication facilities. These explanations work, but they don’t tell the whole story. Rational strategic calculation does not produce a posture in which a nuclear-armed state with the world’s second-largest economy treats a democratic island of 23 million people as a permanent, non-negotiable crisis. But what is rational depends largely on how history has defined you and the ways in which you have defined yourself. The Chinese Communist Party’s posture toward Taiwan is driven not primarily by strategic calculation, at least not in the way it is understood from outside. Its posture is driven by a political trauma the party has consistently chosen to adopt and emphasize: three millennia of Chinese political history, interpreted through what I call the fragmentation pattern. This describes the situation in which a displaced regime establishes a rival power node that continues to claim sovereignty over the whole. It then either reconquers the center or is destroyed. The fact that this binary is false is irrelevant: It is the story that has been embraced, and cynically cultivated. Beijing is finding that echoed civilizational trauma invoked in the name of regime stability is not easily discarded. The resulting ways in which the party is obliged to act are shaped by this narrative. For the United States, the consequence is significant: Deterrence built around imposing costs may fail if Beijing perceives inaction itself as a threat to regime survival. Understanding the historical template through which the Chinese Communist Party interprets Taiwan is therefore necessary to understanding what will deter Beijing and where U.S. strategy is most likely to miscalculate. Taiwan fits the pattern Beijing has chosen to embrace with a precision that should alarm anyone responsible for deterrence planning in the Western Pacific. In 1949, the Chinese Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan after losing the civil war to Chairman Mao Zedong’s Communist forces. They did not establish an independent state. They established the Republic of China on Taiwan and maintained, for decades, that they were the legitimate government of all of China. The Nationalists occupied China’s seat at the United Nations until 1971. They maintained a posture of eventual reconquest well into the Cold War. The rival claim has softened over time as Taiwan democratized and developed its own identity, but the structural fact remains: A defeated regime retreated to a nearby position, claimed sovereign authority, and has persisted for 77 years under foreign protection. A choice hardens into a constraint once it is written into institutions, and this one has been written everywhere. The 2005 Anti-Secession Law put the claim into statute. The 2023 Patriotic Education Law makes reunification a mandatory subject of state education and calls completing it a “sacred duty” of all Chinese, Taiwanese included. A 2022 white paper declared reunification indispensable to national rejuvenation — Xi’s signature slogan. In 2013 Xi told a Taiwanese envoy the problem could not be passed down from one generation to the next, which constitutes a sharp break from Deng Xiaoping’s willingness to wait a thousand years. Each layer raises the price of walking away, however contingent the origins. After three decades of reinforcement, reunification is more tightly bound to regime survival in Beijing than when the campaign began. s posture is driven by the activation of an outdated civilizational threat template that it chose for itself in the name of national unity, then the cost-benefit framework is incomplete. Rational actor theory still holds, but as the Chinese Communist Party applies it to itself, it must be understood that Beijing’s Washington has lately done the opposite. Asked in May whether he would approve a pending $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, President Donald Trump said he was holding it “in abeyance” and that it “depends on China,” adding: “ It’s a very good negotiating chip for us, frankly.” Putting capability on the table while the summits continued is the one trade this argument rules out. Depriving Beijing of rhetorical leverage means rethinking several elements of the current approach. It does not mean prostration: It means exploiting the handcuffs the Chinese Communist Party has placed itself in. First, in the signaling environment, the distinction that matters is between two kinds of statements. Statements about what the United States will do if force is used speak to Beijing’s cost calculation, and that is where deterrence lives. Statements about what Taiwan is, its status, and its place in a contest between democracy and autocracy speak to the template. Washington should make the first kind clearly and often, and the second as seldom as it can. Congressional delegations to Taipei are designed to signal resolve to Beijing. In practice they hand Beijing a pretext. Then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 visit is the clearest case. Its lasting effect was to give Beijing the occasion to erase the median line of the Taiwan Strait: 302 People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed it in August 2022 alone, and by 2025 crossings ran at about 1,500 a year and no longer made the news. Beijing may have wanted a pretext anyway, but the visit supplied it. Actions like this publicly replicate the pattern of foreign powers intervening in what the Chinese Communist Party must process as a threat to itself. A carrier transit of the Taiwan Strait or a quiet weapons sale signals something completely different, and it is a signal that can be understood by Beijing without requiring a high-profile response. Time can be used to the advantage of the United States. The longer Taiwan remains an independent polity, the less existential reunification becomes, provided that the pattern is not constantly re-invoked. The United States cannot abandon Taiwan or cease military preparation, but it must distinguish between signals that deter by raising costs and signals that escalate by feeding the template and creating a public spectacle that the Chinese Communist Party must respond to or lose legitimacy. It must be disciplined about which forces are deployed and when. Quiet capability building deters by changing the military calculus without activating the civilizational narrative, even when the capability being built is devastating. There is a simple litmus test: Does the action change the military balance, or does it only make a statement to which the Chinese Communist Party must respond in escalatory terms? Beijing’s reactions can legitimately be considered as they bear on things that the United States intends to say. Beijing gets no veto over who goes to Taipei. Washington should send people when a visit gains something and hold them back when it would only hand Beijing a pretext. What the United States does is entirely its own business. The main danger of this approach is under-signaling. If the United States only publicly announces things which meaningfully shift the military balance in the Pacific, there is a possibility that the Chinese Communist Party feels emboldened to test established boundaries. Fortunately, this is a problem the current situation is suited to solve. Beijing overreacts reliably to U.S. signaling: Indeed, that is the crux of this entire analysis. That means that any under-signaling can be easily fixed. Persistent under-signaling is rectified with one clear and targeted declaration, but the reverse is not true. Under-signaling is cheap to fix in terms of time, money, and personnel. Over-signaling is not.

results.title: Understanding Global South Perspectives on Taiwan
highlights: Taiwan faces a challenging international environment, beset by mounting pressure from Beijing and mixed signals from Washington. Taiwan’s geopolitical position and its irreplaceable role in global value chains mean that any shift in the cross-Strait status quo would carry profound ramifications for international stability and prosperity. Much has been written about U.S. and “Global North” perspectives on the daunting challenge of maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, but Taiwan’s relationship with the developing world has received comparatively less attention. 1 Taiwan’s interests are also deeply linked to its position in the Global South. It is in the Global South that Beijing seeks to build international support for the most extreme interpretations of its “One China Principle,” secure votes to exclude Taiwan from international organizations, and advance a narrative in which Taiwan and the United States hold exclusive responsibility for deterioration of the cross-Strait status quo. In economic terms, Taiwan relies heavily on foreign workers, particularly from Southeast Asia, and its trade with developing countries comprises a significant 20–25 percent of its total trade activity. 3 As policymakers in G7 capitals work to support Taiwan’s international position and reinforce the cross-Strait status quo, it will be critical to understand the perspectives of Global South stakeholders. Nonetheless, task force members noted that most Global South governments see themselves as neutral players on the Taiwan issue and believe a cross-Strait military crisis would be deeply harmful to their interests, particularly if it resulted in outright conflict between the United States and China. Such a war, they feared, would force Global South countries to choose between these great powers—a geopolitical worst-case scenario for governments that have premised their security and economic growth on welcoming support from both the United States and China, and carefully balancing between them on sensitive issues. Members also expressed concerns that a Taiwan conflict would disrupt Global South countries’ access to key technologies, disturb trade networks, and destabilize the international environment more broadly, increasing the risk they would be drawn into spillover conflicts. Task force members agreed that second to China, the United States is often the most important driver of Taiwan’s standing in the Global South. Several members stressed that Global South leaders perceive U.S. support for Taiwan to have waned over the course of 2025. This change, they noted, may prompt a commensurate shift away from Taiwan in Global South countries. Members noted that some countries, particularly in Latin America, maintain a relationship with Taiwan primarily because they believe this is something Washington wants them to do. Additionally, members pointed to a larger group of Global South countries that endeavor to balance between the United States and China, partnering with both without definitively aligning with either. For these countries, U.S. support for Taiwan serves as a break on how far they are willing to go in endorsing Beijing’s cross-Strait ambitions. Even if these countries support the One China Principle, members noted the countries in question may view this as a compromise between the Chinese and U.S. positions, in part because they do not understand the complexities of either stance. If these governments come to believe the United States no longer supports or prioritizes Taiwan’s international space and the question of cross-Strait peace and stability, members believed their position on Taiwan would swing even further toward Beijing. At the same time, task force participants disagreed on whether Taiwan should openly align itself with the United States in its own diplomatic outreach. In regions where public opinion of the United States is relatively negative, Taiwan should distance itself from the United States and avoid foregrounding its role in U.S.-China competition. In these scenarios, Taiwan will benefit from building relationships with Global South partners in its own right, rather than being weighed down by negative views toward U.S. power projection. In regions where views of the United States are more positive, however, Taiwan will benefit from joint programming and coordinated messaging with the United States. In either case, it will be critical for Taiwan and the United States to carefully assess and coordinate on who should take the lead in making Taiwan’s case. Taiwan cannot compete dollar-for-dollar with China, whose extensive trade networks, overseas investments, and state-backed commercial diplomacy are unparalleled in scale across much of the Global South. Taiwan does maintain a sizeable trade network in its own right, and it ranks in the top 10 trading partners of many Southeast Asian countries. But Taiwan’s trading heft becomes more tenuous beyond Asia, and even close to home, the scale of Taiwan’s trade cannot compete with the incentives Beijing offers. Taiwan’s trade with Global South countries reached $203 billion in 2024, a fraction of their $2.83 trillion in trade with China. 11 In assessing Taiwan’s economic engagement with the Global South, several task force participants again highlighted the important role played by the United States. The vitality of the U.S. economy was perceived as an important proxy for the vitality of Taiwan’s, and many countries see a decision to bet on Taiwan as, more fundamentally, a bet on the United States. Additionally, U.S. investment or commercial diplomacy can supplement and strengthen Taiwanese trade and investment packages. Beyond the economic ramifications of a cross-Strait conflict, some Global South countries—particularly those in Southeast Asia—share certain security interests with Taiwan. In Southeast Asia, Chinese maritime aggression in the South China Sea carries echoes of its coercion in the Taiwan Strait. These commonalities have prompted the Philippines to explore deeper security ties with Taiwan. 18 While other Southeast Asian countries would be loath to invite Beijing’s ire through overt security cooperation with Taiwan, a discreet dialogue on shared maritime challenges may provide a foundation for building trust and understanding over time. - The United States should maintain unwavering support for Taiwan and its international space. Vocal U.S. support for Taiwan raises global awareness of the issue, provides diplomatic cover for other countries to follow suit, and reassures Taiwan’s commercial partners their investments are secure. When the United States appears to deprioritize support for Taiwan, other countries feel there is no geopolitical cost for more fulsomely backing China’s position. in the Global South. Most Global South countries maintain neutrality in the event of a conflict, and a cross-Strait crisis would likely elicit a similar response. However, neutrality does not eliminate the fact that a nearby Taiwan must broaden its engagement and shape its own narrative in the Global South, where its presence and influence remain minimal. This is not about matching China dollar-for-dollar, which would be unrealistic, but about developing a sustained, systemic outreach through developmental, economic, educational, and academic diplomacy. Limiting diplomacy to the United States and the West risks leaving Taiwan isolated in its own region. Despite being more economically developed than most Global South countries and a technological powerhouse, Taiwan’s geographic and strategic position necessitates proactive regional engagement. Episodic diplomacy and neglect would undermine its long-term interests and the wider stability of the region. Strengthening self-sufficiency and preparedness must therefore include robust non-defense engagement, with the Global South as a key focus.

Collins, who is in a tough reelection fight in a state Trump has lost in his three presidential runs, criticized the commander in chief for not adhering to the Russia sanctions legislation he signed into law last month. “I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia. I was a cosponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed but is now not following,” Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, wrote on social media Sunday. She joined three other Senate Republicans and three Democrats in a joint statement blasting Trump for flouting a 2022 statute banning Russian energy imports. “Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Ron Wyden (Ore.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), who is also the ranking member on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” the senators declared, noting that the administration had failed to consult with Congress or offer an explanation to justify the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil as required by law. Republicans acknowledge high diesel costs have become a major political headwind for GOP candidates in battleground races across the country. The senior Senate Republican aide noted that diesel prices have already fallen to $6.27 a gallon from high of $6.53 a gallon in September. “If you look at all the battleground states, the price of diesel, the price of gas are going to be the two big drivers of how people in the middle are going to vote,” the aide added. “It will be huge for farmers around the country who are harvesting right now.” But Alex Jacquez, senior vice president for policy, advocacy and research at the Washington-based economic policy think tank Groundwork Collaborative, said the price of diesel is likely to stay above $6 through Election Day. Jacquez estimated the deal would generate approximately $400 million for the Russian economy. “It’s certainly not insignificant,” he said, but added “it’s not going to be the make-or-break” development in Russia’s war effort, either. The impact on the U.S. economy is also likely to be modest. Jacquez predicted a “minimal” impact on domestic diesel prices. “While 300,000 metric tons — 2.2 billion barrels — sounds like it’s a lot of barrels, which is why Trump is announcing it as such, that’s like half a day of diesel demand in the United States,” he said.

highlights: WASHINGTON, Aug 22 (Reuters) – With the Iran war now at a costly standoff and crises from Ukraine to Gaza still unresolved, President Donald Trump’s ambitious foreign policy agenda appears stuck as he heads into November’s midterm elections. The setbacks are striking for a president who returned to office last year promising to be a “peacemaker” and made resolving international conflicts a centerpiece of his second-term agenda. Trump has grown impatient with reporters’ questions and even U.S. allies. This week, he lashed out at ​reporters pressing him on foreign policy issues and renewed his threat to bomb Oman, a U.S. ally negotiating with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Labor Day, on September 7 ‌this year, is traditionally when election campaigns kick into high gear, and Republicans face the prospect that unresolved conflicts abroad and their economic fallout at home could cost the party its hold on Congress. Trump has called off talks with Tehran after pushing for weeks for a diplomatic solution and announced on Wednesday a new campaign of “economic warfare” against the Islamic Republic in an apparent acknowledgment that months of military attacks have not forced the concessions the U.S. wants to see. As inflation persists and the Iran war drives up gasoline prices, Trump’s approval rating has fallen to another low point with just 33% of Americans in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll approving of his performance. Other efforts to broker peace have also ‌stalled. On Monday, ​Trump’s negotiator and son-in-law Jared Kushner left empty-handed from talks to advance a Gaza peace deal. And an expected visit to Kyiv ⁠by Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff to revive long-stalled ⁠negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine has yet to happen. After a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela’s leader, Trump’s record has become increasingly defined by his stalled diplomatic efforts. The conflict with Iran has weighed “intensely” on the president and there is no consensus inside ​the White House on how to resolve it, one Trump ally said on condition of anonymity. The pressure could increase if investors conclude the war will drag on, driving up U.S. borrowing costs and further constraining Trump’s domestic agenda. Trump has said the economic costs are worth it in order to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon despite Iran’s denials it seeks one. A senior Trump administration official said ​U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade had crippled Iran’s economy and left it “completely broke,” adding, “There are many levers the president can crank harder in the weeks ahead.” Trump has upended traditional diplomatic norms of peacemaking, relying on leveraging America’s economic and military might including with U.S. allies, but that unorthodox style has yielded mixed results. He brought parties to the table with the aim of ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, but the longest war in Europe since World War Two is nowhere near ending, with the latest Russian airstrikes killing 16 people ⁠in the Ukrainian capital on Thursday. In Gaza, mediators fear that intensifying Israeli strikes on the enclave undermine efforts to end the conflict as both Israel and Hamas balk at conditions needed to advance a peace plan Trump forged in October last year. In Lebanon, Israeli airstrikes killed 11 people on Sunday even as a U.S.-mediated peace framework between the two countries remains in effect. One notable success came in ⁠Venezuela, where the U.S. military captured President Nicolas Maduro without U.S. casualties. Analysts ‌say the operation helped convince Trump that joining Israel in attacking Iran would also proceed smoothly. But they also say that proved a miscalculation. They ⁠argue Trump has relied too heavily on applying coercive pressure even though Iran’s leaders have little incentive to back down and reopen the Strait ​of Hormuz despite ‌the country’s weakening economy. Meanwhile, the political clock is ticking, with Trump’s Republican Party facing elections that could cost it control of one or both chambers of Congress and sharply curtail his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years in office. Analysts say Trump’s reliance on coercive pressure can bring adversaries to the table but often fails to produce lasting settlements, a dynamic that may encourage rivals to wait him out. “U.S. adversaries understand that his political clock is shorter than theirs, and that while the United States can apply enormous coercive pressure, it may eventually lose patience,” Aydintasbas said. “Putin, Xi and Iran may therefore want to wait out Washington. After November, the incentive to wait out Trump will become even more pronounced.”

China has dabbled in influence operations as well, though at a smaller scale, and it has typically focused on down-ballot candidates who have criticized the Chinese government. Iran has been another culprit; it successfully hacked the Trump campaign in 2024. All three countries are still pursuing influence operations and could be aided this time by the development of artificial intelligence, which could make such operations more effective and easier to conduct. In the nightmare scenario, these efforts could go beyond poisoning the information environment to disrupting an election or changing vote counts. To limit foreign influence and election interference, the Obama, first Trump, and Biden administrations took steps to prevent foreign governments from exploiting social media and to shore up the integrity of U.S. election infrastructure. The second Trump administration, however, has rolled back many of these changes. With the midterm elections less than four weeks away and control of Congress hanging in the balance, the stakes for the United States are immense. Democracies rest on the ability of their citizens to choose their leaders. If foreign powers can distort the public debate, or worse, change election outcomes, democratic governance is imperiled. To better understand the potential foreign influence and interference threats to the upcoming midterms, I sat down with my Council on Foreign Relations colleague Jessica Brandt for the latest episode of The President’s Inbox podcast. She has deep practical experience facing these challenges, having served as director of the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence during the 2024 U.S. election cycle, where she led the U.S. intelligence community’s efforts to mitigate foreign influence threats. 1. Foreign influence operations and foreign interference efforts are two different things. Foreign influence operations are efforts by foreign governments (or their agents) to shape elections, whether by influencing voter views or preferences, what candidates say or do, or how political parties operate. Influence operations run the gamut: state media, such as China’s Xinhua News Agency and Russia’s RT, that broadcast propaganda; covert media campaigns, such as Russia’s efforts in 2016 [PDF], that push disinformation and misinformation; covert campaign funding, which violates U.S. law and typically relies on noncitizens donating to super PACs and dark money groups; and perception hacking, which uses social media to question the legitimacy of election procedures or their outcomes, including by promoting claims of imaginary election interference. Election interference, on the other hand, refers to covert efforts by foreign governments to disrupt the conduct of elections or the counting of ballots. The first set of actions could include calling in bomb threats to polling places, ransomware attacks that lock up voting data, or hacking into voting databases to alter who is eligible to vote. The second set involves changing or spoiling vote counts by hacking into electronic vote-counting systems. 2. Foreign influence operations have a long history; election interference operations do not. Foreign influence operations in the United States date back to the beginning of the American Republic as foreign governments have periodically sought to shape U.S. elections. The rise of social media, however, has made them far more common. Russia led the way in 2016, with China and Iran soon following its lead. Whether these campaigns have ever swayed an election is notoriously difficult to determine. Too many factors drive voter behavior to isolate the effect of any influence operation. That is why the U.S. government’s investigations of foreign influence operations have focused on their prevalence and methods rather than on [PDF] how effective they might be. No evidence exists that any foreign government has ever run a substantial election interference operation, notwithstanding the allegations of conspiracy theorists. That is not because countries such as Russia, China, and Iran lack the technical capacity to hack at least some election-related databases, networks, and systems. Rather, two practical barriers discourage such efforts. First, states and localities rather than the federal government administer U.S. elections, and as a result, the United States employs a diverse array of voting systems rather than following a single national standard. That diversity greatly complicates any widespread interference campaign. Second, and perhaps more important, foreign governments recognize that election interference operations are exceedingly high-risk. Any attempt to disrupt or change an election could be detected and seen as an act of war. As Jessica put it, foreign governments know that election interference is “a red line for us.” 3. The second Trump administration has canceled or rolled back many of the initiatives that its predecessors launched to discourage influence campaigns and secure U.S. election infrastructure. Jessica noted that the work of groups such as the Foreign Malign Influence Center, the Foreign Influence Task Force at the FBI, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency have all “been scaled back . . . or stood down entirely.” She views these decisions as a major mistake given that Russia, China, and Iran see influence operations as a “low cost” way to sow dissension in the United States and “because they believe it’s working.” As with past elections, it will be impossible to determine to what extent, if at all, these campaigns have succeeded in shaping what voters think. Jessica and I covered a lot of other topics along the way, including the federal government’s efforts to find vulnerabilities in election systems, what role state and local authorities play in keeping U.S. elections secure, and whether artificial intelligence will turbocharge influence operations. I encourage you to give the episode a listen.

results.title: US Midterm Elections 2026: Trump Faces Republican Dissent
highlights: Though a ruling party losing congressional seats in midterms is nothing new, this November’s polls stand out: Republican candidates are distancing themselves from Trump, exposing internal fissures and raising questions about MAGA’s future. The 2026 US midterm elections are less than four weeks away, and the political environment is becoming increasingly difficult for Donald Trump’s Republican Party. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats will be up for election on November 3. Polling increasingly points to Democratic gains in the House, while the Senate race remains more uncertain. Economic dissatisfaction, rising energy costs and the political fallout from the Iran conflict are putting pressure on the Republican Party. This does not necessarily make 2026 an exceptional election. Historically, the President’s party tends to lose congressional seats in midterm elections. Since 1938, the President’s party has lost House ground in 20 of 22 midterm elections. In fact, during Trump’s first midterms in 2018, Republicans lost 41 seats in the House. It’s a vulnerability Trump is well aware of. What is particularly interesting about the 2026 US midterm elections is that Republican candidates in 41 of the 62 competitive congressional races have sought to distance themselves from President Donald Trump, according to a Reuters review, amid concerns over electoral implications of his policies. The Iran conflict, rising fuel prices, data centres and beef imports have emerged as points of contention. Republican unease with Trump has become visible not only in campaign strategy but also in congressional action. Some members of his party have joined efforts to limit his war powers, challenged the administration over the release of Epstein-related files, and aspects of tariff policies, including those affecting Canada. Republican candidates have also reduced Trump’s visibility in their campaigns by removing his endorsements from their websites and avoiding joint appearances. Again, such distancing is not unprecedented; Republicans adopted similar strategies during the 2018 midterm elections. However, the 2026 midterms stand out for the breadth of the distancing and the range of policy disagreements involved. With Trump’s approval ratings remaining weak, his early campaign stops have also drawn attention. Rather than prioritising competitive districts that could determine control of Congress, he has been holding rallies in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Oklahoma, and Alabama. If Democrats regain control of the House while Republicans retain the Senate, as it happened after the 2018 midterm elections, the immediate consequences would likely centre on increased congressional oversight rather than a fundamental reversal of Trump’s foreign policy. Democrats could hold hearings, demand documents, and investigate the legal, humanitarian, and migration-related implications of the administration’s policies, including the costs and legal basis of military operations. They could also use the appropriations process to seek restrictions or conditions on military funding, although such measures would face obstacles in the Senate and could be subject to a presidential veto. Impeachment proceedings could also re-emerge, but convicting Trump and removing him from office would require the support of two-thirds of the senators present. The balance of power would change more substantially, however, if Democrats gained control of both chambers. A Democratic Senate could complicate the passage of legislation and funding measures and make confirmation of future presidential nominees more difficult. However, this possibility remains highly uncertain. Assuming they retain their current seats, Democrats would need a net gain of at least four seats to secure a 51-seat Senate majority. The 2026 midterms could provide an early indication of the challenges MAGA (Make America Great Again) may face in maintaining its cohesion beyond Trump. The MAGA movement is a populist, nationalist faction within the broader Republican Party wing that centres on Donald Trump’s “America First” agenda, which prioritises economic protectionism through tariffs, strict anti-immigration policies, scepticism towards foreign intervention, and a disruptive anti-establishment posture. Trump’s MAGA movement has indeed united a diverse coalition of economic nationalists, immigration hardliners, religious conservatives, and anti-establishment voters within the Republican Party—often referred to as Grand Old Party (GOP)—whose priorities do not always align. However, growing dissatisfaction with aspects of Trump’s policy record, alongside his declining popularity and efforts by an increasing number of Republican candidates to distance themselves from him ahead of the 2026 midterms point to growing tensions within the GOP. And with the Constitution barring Trump from being elected to another presidential term in 2028, the question of succession becomes increasingly significant. The question, therefore, is whether MAGA can retain its cohesion under new leadership or whether competing factions will emerge, each claiming to represent the true heir to “America First”. Trump’s departure could expose differences within the coalition that his leadership has held together. Such fragmentation, if it occurs, would not necessarily signal a decline in MAGA’s broader political influence. The evolution of earlier conservative movements, such as the Tea Party, offers a useful historical reference, illustrating how a movement’s ideas can continue to shape the Republican Party even as it loses its distinct organisational identity.
