results.title: 2026 US Midterm Elections: Key Issues & Debates
highlights: WHAT ARE THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS & WHY ARE THEY IMPORTANT? On November 3, 2026, the United States (US) will hold its midterm elections. Held two years into a president’s four-year term, the elections mark the halfway point of a presidency. They provide voters with the opportunity to elect the members of the two chambers of Congress – the House of Representatives and the Senate. Congress plays a central role in shaping US domestic and foreign policy, given their mandate of passing laws, approving government spending, and exercising oversight over the executive branch. In many ways, the midterms also serve as a review of the incumbent president’s first two years in office. The midterms are taking place against a paradoxical backdrop: both the Republican and Democratic parties remain highly polarized against one another, while also experiencing significant tensions internally within their own parties as well. It remains difficult to decenter President Trump and his policies from the future trajectory of the Republican Party, despite growing internal opposition against tarrifs and involvement in wars abroad, as well as the rising costs of living as a result. The Democrats, on the other hand, remain fractured and without clear leadership capable of rallying the different factions of the party together. Despite Trump’s grip over the party, Republicans are increasingly split between choosing to continue to support him publicly, which will risk their prospects in the 2028 elections, and deciding to break away completely to spearhead a future revival of the party instead. The MAGA movement continues to command strong support among many voters, but tensions have emerged within the movement, with more influential voices willing to challenge the president’s agenda. These disagreements have made it harder for Republicans to have a more united policy agenda ahead of the midterms. The current state of the economy is the most defining issue, with 47% of registered voters stating that the cost of living will be the main deciding factor of who they endorse in the elections. 1 While inflation has indeed fallen since Trump took office, the cost of goods remains high, with gas prices at almost their highest levels since 2022, and consumer prices 3.4% higher than in August 2025. For Republicans running in the midterms, their campaigns have focused on framing the Trump administration’s economic policies, including tax cuts, investments, and efforts to support American businesses, as wins. However, the administration itself still faces the challenge of convincing voters that these policies are actually improving their day-to-day lives. Trump has sought to address affordability directly, promising a $5,000 payment to all adults if Republicans win the midterms, in a highly controversial move. The conflict’s economic consequences have made the issue of the war particularly significant for voters. Disruptions to energy markets and higher oil prices have added to existing concerns over the economy. For voters, the issue is not mainly about foreign policy and national security, but about the price they are forced to pay for a conflict that is increasingly impacting their everyday lives. Democrats have criticized the administration’s policy on Iran, questioning the war’s objectives, costs, duration, and broader consequences. They have also criticized Trump’s launching of the war without gaining prior congressional approval. Meanwhile, some Republicans stand firmly with the Trump administration on this file, viewing the war as a historic opportunity to combat Iran’s ability to harm US interests, as well as to dismantle its nuclear program. However, the unplanned consequences of the war, including the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on US bases, have led to divisions within the Republican Party itself. The inconsistency in the White House’s approach has caused further polarization on the issue, given early promises of the war taking no more than a few weeks back in March currently culminating in a dangerous stalemate of neither war nor peace. Some Republican Senators, including Thom Tillis, voted alongside the Democrats to advance a resolution aimed at limiting Trump’s powers on Iran. Republican representative of the state of Kentucky, Thomas Massie, has also attempted to impeach current Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the war. Immigration remains one of the Republican Party’s most prominent priority issues. Many Republicans have praised and backed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies, including the expanded use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). In August 2026 alone, over 50,000 people were arrested across the US. However, the issue has also exposed some internal divisions. Republican Representative Maria Salazar has criticized aspects of current immigration policies, underscoring that enforcement has “gone too far.” Meanwhile, Democrats have sought to appeal to their voters by highlighting the humanitarian and legal consequences of the administration’s policies. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be House Speaker if the Democrats win a majority, has strongly criticized the Trump administration’s use of ICE, arguing that taxpayer money should be used to make life more affordable instead. More recently, Democratic representative Delia Ramirez proposed a bill which calls for the dismantling of the US Department of Homeland Security and the elimination of ICE. The outcome of the midterms will shape the political landscape in which Trump governs during the remaining two years of his second term. The impact will depend on which chamber each party will control, as the House and Senate have different constitutional powers. If Republicans retain control of the House, Trump would have greater support for his legislative agenda, particularly on taxation and government spending. Additionally, a Republican Senate would give him a clearer path to confirming cabinet officials, ambassadors, and federal judges. If Republicans control both chambers, Trump would face fewer obstacles in Congress and have greater ability to coordinate legislation, spending, and appointments till the end of his term. If Democrats win the House, they would gain greater power to investigate the administration and block parts of Trump’s legislative agenda. A Democratic House would also increase the chances of Trump’s impeachment, since the chamber has the constitutional power to impeach officials. A Democratic Senate could slow or reject presidential appointments. If they control both chambers, Trump would face substantially greater opposition and scrutiny through congressional investigations. The results could also affect Trump’s foreign policy agenda. A Republican-majority Congress would generally give the administration more freedom to pursue its priorities, including major defense agreements and arms sales. A Democratic House or Senate, however, could subject military operations and arms deals to greater scrutiny, using congressional procedures to challenge proposed weapons sales. 3 This could also affect Trump’s approach to ongoing or potentially new wars. A divided Congress, with each party controlling one chamber, would create a more complicated balance of power. Trump could retain support for some policies while facing opposition on others, depending on which party will control which chamber. about control of Congress, the elections will also be an early test for the politicians competing for the presidency in 2028. The 2026 midterms may be the first real contest of the 2028 presidential race, shaping the political environment in which the next presidential campaign will unfold. The results could determine which party enters 2028 with greater momentum, while forcing both sides to reassess their strategies, leadership, and appeal to voters.

results.title: Is Trump sacrificing Ukraine for congressional elections?
highlights: Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump in the White House The agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian Vladimir Putin on the export of diesel caused dissatisfaction in Ukraine. Energy prices are the main topic in the US mid-term elections and Trump is looking for a scapegoat to cover up the bad economic situation Agreement of the American President Donald Trump and the Russian president Vladimir Putin about the export of Russian diesel to the world market caused outrage in Ukraine. According to the American portal Axios, the agreement is interpreted in Kiev as a response to the Ukrainian leadership's refusal to stop attacks on Russian refineries. Trump further raised tensions by saying that it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader who could make a deal. Such words reopened the discussion about the attitude of the US administration towards Volodymyr Zelensky and the future of US support to Ukraine. The announcement of the agreement came at the exact when Ukrainian, American and European representatives were holding in Miami. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky did not hide his displeasure For the Ukrainian leadership, this is not the first serious conflict with the Trump administration. Already in February 2025, there was an open verbal conflict in the Oval Office, when Trump told Zelensky that he "doesn't have the cards in his hands right now." That meeting was followed by a temporary suspension of arms deliveries and the exchange of intelligence between the two countries. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during the negotiations in Miami again mentioned the possibility of suspending intelligence cooperation due to Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. DW interlocutors mostly associate Trump's increased attacks on Ukraine with the congressional elections that will be held on November 3. In those elections, the entire convocation of the House of Representatives and a third of the Senate are elected, and high fuel prices have become one of the central themes of the campaign. Ivan Us from the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv believes that the Republicans are threatened with a serious political blow due to energy prices. "Donald Trump wants at all costs to divert attention from the fact that the high prices are connected to his war against Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. For that he needs a scapegoat and he decided to make it Ukraine", according to Us. Mihajlo Hončar also believes that the agreement primarily benefits Moscow. "The whole diesel thing looks like Putin's veiled plea to Trump to put more pressure on Ukraine," the analyst said. In his opinion, Ukraine should simultaneously work together with Germany, Denmark, Great Britain and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel to the USA politically and logistically unfeasible. He believes that Ukrainian diplomacy should maintain contacts with Republicans and the MAGA movement, where criticism of Trump's agreement with Putin is already appearing. Some Republicans warn that additional revenues from diesel sales could indirectly benefit Iran and other Russian allies. The US does not rule out the possibility that Trump's decision will end up in court. Republican Sen. Tom Tillish told NBC that there is a possibility that the president is violating the 2022 law that banned the import of Russian oil and other energy products. In Uso's view, announcements about the possible withholding of weapons and intelligence are more about creating political impression than actual policy change. "Such statements are aimed at convincing the markets that Washington is taking decisive steps and thus influencing energy prices," according to Us. All three experts agree that Kiev should withstand the pressure at least until the US elections are over. Oleksandr Krajiv believes that Trump may soften his approach after the election. Leaving Ukraine, he warns, would send a signal of weakness to China, which is closely following developments around Taiwan. Mihajlo Hončar reminds that some Republicans in the Senate and the House of Representatives are already speaking out against the agreement with Russia. He also mentions the legislative proposal initiated by Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick with the aim of blocking the purchase of Russian energy products. "Despite all the threats and possible temporary measures against Kiev, it is unlikely that Trump will go much further. The situation should not be viewed apocalyptically," Honchar believes. In his opinion, the American pressure could also have an unwanted consequence for Washington: an additional approach of Ukraine to its European allies.

results.title: Senate Foreign Relations Members Rebuke Trump Over Russian Diesel Deal — The World Signal
highlights: Seven senators on the Foreign Relations Committee condemned Trump's deal with Putin to allow Russian diesel imports, calling it a violation of law and a financial lifeline to Moscow. A bipartisan group of seven senators on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee issued a sharp rebuke of President Donald Trump’s recent agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which would lift sanctions and permit Russian oil to flow into global markets. The statement, released Sunday, accused the administration of violating federal law and undermining Ukraine’s defense against Russian aggression. “Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” the senators wrote. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies.” The statement was signed by Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, and Ron Wyden of Oregon, alongside Republicans Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah. The group argued that Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports directly contravenes the 2022 law and that the administration failed to consult Congress or provide any legal justification as required by statute. The controversy erupted Friday when Trump announced on Truth Social that after a conversation with Putin, Russia would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” The move has drawn criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, with some Republicans joining Democrats in expressing alarm. Sen. Tillis warned that the deal undermines ongoing efforts to tighten sanctions on Moscow, while others have called for a bipartisan bill to block Russian oil imports. The decision comes amid months of rising diesel prices, which have put political pressure on Republicans as the midterm elections approach. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the price hikes, while some administration officials point to the conflict in Iran. The White House has not yet responded to the senators’ statement. The bipartisan pushback signals growing unease within Congress over Trump’s foreign policy posture toward Russia, even as the president maintains a firm grip on the GOP base. The senators’ demand for an immediate reversal sets up a potential legal and political clash over the scope of executive authority on sanctions. Bipartisan fury over the diesel deal has been building since Friday, with some lawmakers calling for hearings and legislative action. As the administration weighs its next move, the standoff underscores the delicate balance between energy prices, election-year politics, and the ongoing war in Ukraine. The senators’ letter makes clear that any attempt to bypass Congress on Russian energy imports will face fierce resistance from both parties.

results.title: ‘The cost to us, the United States, is high’: Trump’s ‘financial lifeline’ diesel deal with Putin sparks bipartisan backlash in Congress – DNYUZ
highlights: ‘The cost to us, the United States, is high’: Trump’s ‘financial lifeline’ diesel deal with Putin sparks bipartisan backlash in Congress – DNYUZ ‘The cost to us, the United States, is high’: Trump’s ‘financial lifeline’ diesel deal with Putin sparks bipartisan backlash in Congress October 13, 2026 in News The stark assessment years ago from Nancy Pelosi echoed anew after Trump’s surprise announcement last week that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. as a way to ease sky-high prices at the pumps for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. Trump’s diesel deal with Putin has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats as fueling Russia’s war against Ukraine, violating existing U.S. laws and drawing the U.S. closer to Russia. It joins a growing list of instances in which the Republican president has sided with Putin, often at the expense of Ukraine — and America’s own standing. It’s not at all clear the Trump-Putin deal will deliver the supply boost the president is seeking to bring down prices. Energy experts have said the flow of Russian diesel is unlikely to lower prices in the U.S., which have escalated largely due to disruptions from the U.S. war against Iran. But the agreement underlines a message at home and abroad that Trump is an unreliable ally as Ukraine battles Russia. A bipartisan group of six senators urged Trump over the weekend to reverse course, saying the U.S. “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline.” Trump, however, held fast to his deal with Putin and lashed out, blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for America’s high diesel costs and asserting he should step aside — something Ukraine’s leader has no intention of doing. Trump also insisted that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Zelenskyy saying that Moscow continued to strike his country s energy sites. Congress voted to halt Russian imports, but Trump has other plans Congress swiftly approved legislation at the outset of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in spring of 2022 to ban the import of Russian energy products, which are widely viewed as providing the financial fuel for Putin’s military assault on Ukraine. The bill passed the House on an overwhelming 414-17 vote and the Senate without a single senator opposed. The law says the president can seek to lift the prohibition if an agreement has been reached to withdraw Russian troops from Ukraine and cease military activity. Such a proposal would need to be reviewed by Congress and to have been “accepted by the free and independent government of Ukraine.” More recently, Congress last month approved a sweeping Russian sanctions bill, named after the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would slap tariffs on countries that continue importing Russian oil. Trump signed the bill into law. The bulk of the law’s provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration’s 30-day review period. But such action now appears to be in question since Trump’s diesel deal with Putin will allow the flow of Russian energy. In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senate leaders from both parties last week said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. But that was before Trump announced his deal with Putin, which he said would unleash hundreds of tons of diesel. Trump, Russia and Pelosi’ Almost seven years ago this week, Pelosi stood before Trump and a roomful of U.S. officials during a heated White House meeting and leveled her accusation, suggesting the president’s policy favored Putin. The powerful House speaker led the first impeachment of Trump on corruption charges over his administration’s decision to withhold congressionally approved aid to Ukraine in 2019 as it faced Russian aggression at its border. Trump was later acquitted by the Senate. Since Trump’s return to the White House, he has seesawed between pressuring Zelenskyy to make concessions and showing frustration with Putin’s hard-line stance on the war. Trump often complains that he thought his good relationship with his Russian counterpart would have made it easier to end the war. A year ago, Trump reversed his long-held position that Ukraine would have to give up land and suggested it could win back all the territory it has lost to Russia — only later to call on Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are” and end the war. In July, Trump praised Zelenskyy and Ukraine for their wartime resilience. But by September, Trump was expressing frustration about strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump insisted Monday the sides agreed to a ceasefire on the energy systems. “They agreed,” Trump said. “Because I said, ‘You agree.’” When pressed about the attacks by Russia, Trump said he’d have to take a look, “because there’s been violations on both sides.”

results.title: The 2026 US midterm elections and the future of American support for Ukraine - On Line Opinion - 13/11/2025
highlights: The 2026 United States midterm elections are poised to become a decisive moment in shaping Washington's foreign policy, particularly regarding the ongoing war in Ukraine. Following a period of strained relations and fluctuating military assistance during President Donald Trump's second term, the political composition of Congress after November 2026 could fundamentally alter the trajectory of US engagement in Eastern Europe. If Democrats regain control of one or both chambers of Congress, they would likely reassert strong bipartisan and institutional backing for Kyiv, reversing recent reductions in aid and signalling a renewed American commitment to defending democratic values abroad. The most recent local elections in 2025 revealed significant Republican setbacks, as Democrats achieved sweeping victories across major US cities and key governorships. These results suggest growing voter disillusionment with the GOP's internal divisions and its association with Trump's polarising leadership. Should these trends persist into the 2026 midterms, Democrats have a realistic chance of reclaiming control of the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate. Such a shift would not remove Trump from office but would critically constrain his authority, especially in foreign policy and defence. Congress wields powerful tools to shape national security through control of the budget, appropriations, and oversight functions. A Democratic resurgence could therefore reinvigorate US support for Ukraine and restore predictability to Washington's global posture. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Trump has markedly reduced US involvement in Ukraine. He has repeatedly paused or cancelled previously approved military aid packages, citing concerns about domestic stockpile depletion and the financial burden of prolonged overseas commitments. His administration replaced the rapid Presidential Drawdown Authority, used extensively under President Biden, with a slower NATO-based framework known as the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL). These bureaucratic changes have limited the flow of weapons and equipment to Kyiv. Reports of tense exchanges between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggestions that Ukraine should cede the Donbas region to Russia, have further strained relations. Consequently, total US assistance has fallen sharply from Biden-era levels of approximately $200 billion, comprising military, financial, and humanitarian aid, over three years, to a fraction of that amount. If Democrats regain control of Congress in 2026, one of their most powerful instruments for influencing Ukraine policy would be the federal budget. Congress holds the constitutional "power of the purse," allowing it to allocate and direct funds even when the executive branch is resistant. A Democratic majority could enact binding appropriations requiring specific levels of military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine. While President Trump could attempt to delay the release of these funds, such action would risk violating spending laws and provoking political backlash. The precedent is clear: even the Republican-led Senate in 2025 approved $1 billion in Ukraine support with broad bipartisan consensus. A Democratic Congress would likely expand on this model, introducing multi-year funding to ensure consistent aid and prioritising the swift delivery of defensive systems. In addition to its financial authority, Congress could legislate new constraints on presidential discretion regarding aid distribution. A Democratic majority might pass laws preventing the president from freezing or cancelling assistance without formal justification, thereby institutionalising safeguards against political interference. Although President Trump could veto such legislation, a sufficiently united Congress - especially one drawing support from pro-Ukraine Republicans - could override the veto. Similar bipartisan cooperation has emerged in the past, notably in defence spending and NATO-related votes, where lawmakers set aside partisan divides to protect strategic US interests abroad. A Democratic Congress would also likely enhance oversight and accountability concerning Ukraine policy. Through investigative hearings and committee inquiries, legislators could scrutinise any delays, diversions, or mismanagement of funds within the executive branch. Such oversight would not only compel greater transparency from the administration but also reassure Ukraine and America's NATO allies that congressional intent is being upheld. By ensuring that appropriated funds are delivered promptly and effectively, Congress would reaffirm the reliability of the United States as a global partner committed to democratic defence. Finally, an empowered Congress could act decisively to remove bureaucratic bottlenecks that have slowed aid transfers under the Trump administration. Legislative directives could compel the Pentagon and State Department to streamline delivery mechanisms, eliminating red tape that has hindered the shipment of essential systems such as Patriot interceptors, HIMARS launchers, and advanced ammunition. By reducing administrative delays, a Democratic-controlled Congress would not only accelerate Ukraine's access to critical military resources but also demonstrate the efficiency and resolve of US governance in moments of international crisis. A reinvigorated US commitment to Ukraine would likely restore the scale and intensity of assistance seen during the Biden administration. Annual military aid could return to levels between $50 and $65 billion, providing Ukraine with the material strength necessary to sustain its defence and counteroffensive operations. Equally important would be the introduction of multi-year funding commitments extending through 2027 and 2028. Such predictability would allow Kyiv to plan long-term strategies with confidence, reducing its dependence on short-term political cycles in Washington and signalling to both allies and adversaries that US support is enduring. attacks. Politically and diplomatically, Washington's backing would reinforce Ukraine's sovereignty by opposing any settlement involving coerced territorial concessions. Together, these measures would not only strengthen Ukraine's ability to defend itself but also reaffirm the United States' broader commitment to upholding international law, deterring aggression, and sustaining the Despite these possibilities, even a Democratic-controlled Congress would face structural limits. The President retains significant authority over foreign policy implementation, including the timing of aid delivery and the conduct of diplomatic negotiations. Trump could still obstruct or delay assistance through bureaucratic channels or executive orders. Nonetheless, Congress possesses tools to counter such obstruction, chiefly through conditional appropriations, public pressure, and the threat of impeachment if aid were unlawfully withheld. The likely outcome would be a tense but functional equilibrium: a Democratic Congress pressing assertively for Ukraine's defence, and a resistant executive gradually compelled to yield under political and legal pressure. The 2026 US midterm elections will not only determine the balance of domestic political power but may also redefine America's moral and strategic posture on the global stage. A Democratic resurgence in Congress would almost certainly strengthen Ukraine's position, restoring predictable and substantial US assistance while reaffirming that America remains steadfast in the defence of freedom and sovereignty. For Ukraine, the stakes could not be higher. Democratic control of Congress would mean renewed lifelines of military aid, diplomatic support, and moral solidarity. For the United States, it would reaffirm a long-standing principle: that the defence of democracy abroad is inseparable from its preservation at home.

And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.” Trump’s remark rattled Argentine markets, which had been buoyed by the support package recently announced by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The centrepiece of that deal is a $20-billion US currency swap with Argentina’s central bank, exchanging stable U.S. dollars for volatile pesos. Bessent said at Tuesday’s meeting that the package — full details of which have not been announced — is predicated on the continuance of economic policies favoured by the Trump administration. While details of the agreement remain unclear, the bailout could offer the libertarian Milei a much-needed political boost as he works to stave off a deepening economic crisis and shore up his party’s support. He suffered a major setback last month as voters in an election in Buenos Aires province registered their frustration with rising unemployment, contracting economic activity and brewing corruption scandals. Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party hopes to improve its standing in Argentina’s Congress as it holds midterm legislative elections on Oct. 26. The economic lifeline for Argentina marks an unusual move for the U.S., particularly under an administration that has largely eschewed major foreign interventions. It has slashed foreign and humanitarian aid across the board and shifted the focus in U.S. policy for the Russia-Ukraine war toward emphasizing European purchases of American military weapons and equipment, with no new funding in congressional bills for Ukraine. The Argentinian assistance underscores the extent to which the Trump administration is willing to support a political ally who has cultivated strong ties with the president and American conservatives in recent years. Milei, whom Trump has described as his “favourite president,” was one of two world leaders onstage during Trump’s inauguration. The policy has drawn criticism at home. Many Democratic lawmakers have accused Trump of prioritizing foreign bailouts and investor protections while the U.S. government is in a partial shutdown, in its 15th day as of Wednesday. purchases from U. has threatened in its trade relationship with the shift in Chinese purchasing a negotiation . He said this month he hoped to discuss soybeans soon with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping. The White House has framed the Argentinian bailout deal as a strategic effort to stabilize a key regional ally, but it is arguably Trump’s most overt call to action concerning another country’s domestic affairs. At the same time, as Trump admitted at the White House on Tuesday, “we don’t have to do it.” “It’s not going to make a big difference for our country,” he said. This summer, Trump was angered by the trial and subsequent conviction of Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro, an ally. The U.S. hiked tariffs on many Brazilian goods as a result of what Trump called a “witch hunt,” sanctioned the judge overseeing the case and took away the visas of several Brazilian officials. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva called the new tariffs “unacceptable blackmail,” though officials from both countries have cooled down their rhetoric, with delegations expected to meet soon to talk trade. Trump has been sensitive to what he perceives as election interference in the U.S., including the since-shuttered criminal prosecutions that proceeded when he was a private citizen between presidential terms. results.title: Trump's diesel deal with Putin draws criticism from a frustrated Congress - LA NACION
highlights: Trump's diesel deal with Putin draws criticism from a frustrated Congress - LA NACION The president faces bipartisan backlash over a Russian diesel deal; critics argue the agreement violates federal law with Putin draws The stark assessment years ago from Nancy Pelosi echoed anew after Trump’s surprise announcement last week that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. as a way to ease sky-high prices at the pumps for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. Trump’s diesel deal with Putin has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats as fueling Russia’s war against Ukraine , violating existing U.S. laws and drawing the U.S. closer to Russia. It joins a growing list of instances where the president has sided with Putin , often at the expense of Ukraine — and America’s own standing. It’s not at all clear the Trump-Putin deal will deliver the supply boost the president is seeking to bring down prices. Energy experts have said the flow of Russian diesel is unlikely to lower prices in the U.S., which have escalated largely due to disruptions from the U.S. war against Iran . But the agreement underlines a message at home and abroad that Trump is an unreliable ally as Ukraine battles Russia. A bipartisan group of six senators urged Trump over the weekend to reverse course, saying the U.S. “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline.” Trump, however, held fast to his deal with Putin and lashed out, blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for America's high diesel costs and asserting he should step aside — something Ukraine's leader has no intention of doing. Asked about Republican criticism of the Russia deal, Trump said they "can’t really be serious.” Trump also insisted that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Zelenskyy saying that Moscow continued to strike his country’s energy sites. Congress voted to halt Russian imports, but Trump has other plans Congress swiftly approved legislation at the outset of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in spring of 2022 to ban the import of Russian energy products, which are widely viewed as providing the financial fuel for Putin’s military assault on Ukraine. The bill passed the House on an overwhelming 414-17 vote and the Senate without a single senator opposed. The law says the president can seek to lift the prohibition if an agreement had been reached to withdraw Russian troops from Ukraine and cease military activity. Such a proposal would need to be reviewed by Congress and to have been “accepted by the free and independent government of Ukraine.” “Trump is directly violating that law,” said Rep. Lloyd Doggett, D-Texas, the bill's chief sponsor, in a statement Monday. More recently, Congress last month approved a sweeping Russian sanctions bill , named after the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would slap tariffs on countries that continue importing Russian oil. Trump signed the bill into law. The bulk of the law’s provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration’s 30-day review period. But such action now appears to be in question since Trump's diesel deal with Putin will allow the flow of Russian energy. In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio , Senate leaders from both parties last week said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. But that was before Trump announced his deal with Putin, which he said would unleash hundreds of tons of diesel. Trump, Russia and Pelosi’s stand Almost seven years ago this week, Pelosi stood before Trump and a roomful of U.S. officials during a heated White House meeting and leveled her accusation, suggesting the president's policy favored Putin. The powerful House speaker led the first impeachment of Trump on corruption charges over his administration’s decision to withhold congressionally approved aid to Ukraine in 2019 as it faced Russian aggression at its border. Trump was later acquitted by the Senate. Since Trump's return to the White House, he has seesawed between pressuring Zelenskyy to make concessions and showing frustration with Putin’s hardline stance on the war. Trump often complains that he thought his good relationship with his Russian counterpart would have made it easier to end the war. A year ago, Trump reversed his long-held position that Ukraine would have to give up land and suggested it could win back all the territory it has lost to Russia — only later to call on Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are” and end the war. In July, Trump praised Zelenskyy and Ukraine for their wartime resilience. But by September, Trump was expressing frustration about strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump insisted Monday the sides agreed to a ceasefire on the energy systems. “They agreed,” Trump said. “Because I said, 'You agree.'” When pressed about the attacks by Russia, Trump said he'd have to take a look, "because there’s been violations on both sides.”

results.title: Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before midterms
highlights: Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before midterms Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections Trump announced a new deal for diesel with Russian President Putin on Friday With elections that will decide control of Congress just weeks away and American voters already casting ballots in some battlegrounds, President Donald Trump has turned his eyes overseas – and to Russia, in particular - for help tackling one of his most pressing problems. A whirlwind weekend started on Friday afternoon, as Trump announced a new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide the US with hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel in the coming months. Polls suggest they view the Iran War as the leading cause for their woes, and overall support for Trump, and approval of his handling of the war and the US economy in particular, has dropped precipitously. Trump heralded his Russian deal in a Truth Social post as bringing "lower prices for Americans," while he ordered his Treasury Department to suspend US restrictions that prevented Russian diesel from being sold on global markets. Two days later, Trump was back on his social media website, touting a new energy ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had no advanced notice of agreement, although he said his nation would abide by it. Russia, for its part, was silent. And on Sunday night, it launched a new wave of attacks on Ukrainian power plants. Trump and Zelensky have had a tumultuous relationship throughout his second term. The American president alternates between blaming Russia and Ukraine for the continuing conflict he previously said would be easy to end once he returned to the White House. In recent days, Zelensky has been the primary target of Trump's ire, as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil infrastructure have contributed to worldwide energy shortages. On Saturday, Trump told reporters at the White House that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. And both the Financial Times and CNN have reported that the US has threatened to cut off arms sales and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Zelensky does not halt attacks on Russian refineries. Zelensky "better damn well stop," Trump said. It now appears Trump's celebration of the "energy truce" may have been a familiar move for this president, touting an agreement before it had been sealed and delivered. In the past, for instance, he has prematurely announced Middle East ceasefires and sweeping peace agreements. Whether it is on the president's part diplomacy or a savvy negotiating tactic to push a deal across the finish line, the result has been to set off a scramble as the world decides what it means – and how to react. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has become a vocal critic of the president's on the international stage, offered "strong support" for the energy ceasefire, but condemned the diesel deal as undermining peace and stability in Europe and helping Russia to finance its "illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine". In the US, Trump's diesel announcement prompted similar concern, even among members of his own party. Four Republican senators joined with Democrats in a letter calling on the president to "immediately reverse course". "Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the senators wrote in a statement released on Sunday. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law." What could be worse for the president than the criticisms is that the announced ceasefire has had little effect on the price of diesel, which continues to sit below its record highs but still well above $6 a gallon. Meanwhile, as the latest twists in the Russia-Ukraine conflict unfolded, new violence in the Middle East threaten to further strain global energy markets, regardless of what happens with Russian oil. A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on airports and energy infrastructure that killed at least 13 over the weekend, have threatened to escalate a decade-long conflict that had been simmering throughout the US-Iran war. The US-Iran war was a conflict that none of the Arab nations in region wanted, he said, and the latest Houthi offensive was a foreseeable result. With the US and Iran currently in an extended stand-off, any new hostilities could lead to more regional conflict and send oil prices soaring once more. In recent weeks, Trump has pointed to Ukraine, not the Middle East, as the primary source of the world's energy woes. He cites increased oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively shut by Iran's military threat. There is only one president at a time, however. And when American voters casts their ballots they tend to hold those who are currently in power responsible. After a rough weekend that again proved there are no easy fixes to the global energy crisis, that may be the worst news of all for the US president.

results.title: US Midterm Elections 2024: Key Races, Issues, and What's at Stake for Trump (2026)
highlights: US Midterm Elections 2024: Key Races, Issues, and What's at Stake for Trump (2026) The High-Stakes Chess Match: Why the Upcoming Midterms Are Not Just About Congress As we creep closer to the November ballot box, the political air in Washington feels heavy with anticipation. Personally, I think it is far too easy to view midterms as merely a report card for a sitting president, but this election cycle carries a unique atmospheric pressure. What makes this particular political moment fascinating is how rapidly public sentiment can pivot when international chaos intersects with domestic wallet pain. In my opinion, we are watching a classic political collision course unfold in slow motion, where every single congressional district becomes a battleground for the soul of American governance. If you take a step back and think about it, a president's approval rating has always been the ultimate political barometer, yet watching Donald Trump's numbers slide into the high thirties reveals something much deeper about the modern electorate. What many people don't realize is that voters do not just register disapproval; they weaponize it at the ballot box during midterms. From my perspective, the modern voter is perpetually exhausted by a compounding cycle of crises, and when the administration's numbers slump below 40%, it acts as a clarion call for the opposition. A detail that I find especially interesting is how historical patterns suggest the ruling party almost always bleeds seats, a gravitational pull that even the most formidable political movements struggle to defy. - The Historical Penalty: The president's party loses an average of 27 House seats in midterm cycles, a trend stretching back decades. - The Tipping Point: Approval ratings sitting under 40% typically open the floodgates for unexpected upsets in traditionally safe districts. - The Enthusiasm Gap: Low presidential numbers often breed fierce urgency among the opposition while dampening baseline turnout for the incumbent. When you look at the raw math of Congress, the fragility of political power becomes painfully clear. What this really suggests is that democracy in America often hinges on a handful of razor-thin margins in places most voters couldn't find on a map. In the House, where a single-digit shift can completely flip the speaker's gavel, the entire apparatus rests on just a couple of dozen toss-up districts. Personally, I find it astounding that billions of dollars and years of political strategy culminate in races where the margin of victory could literally come down to a few thousand independent voters in suburban neighborhoods. If you examine the Senate battlegrounds, the challenge for Democrats trying to break through in traditionally deep-red states like Texas or Ohio feels like climbing a vertical glass wall, yet changing voter demographics keep making those climbs surprisingly plausible. One thing that immediately stands out about this election cycle is how quickly grand political promises can be unmade by unforeseen global events. Trump campaigned heavily on making America affordable again, but watching gas prices spike to four dollars a gallon following the conflict with Iran demonstrates how vulnerable domestic politics are to foreign shocks. What many people fail to appreciate is that foreign policy decisions are rarely abstract to the average voter; they are measured directly at the gas pump and the grocery checkout counter. In my opinion, the administration's vulnerability here is not just about the policy itself, but about the jarring contrast between early campaign rhetoric and the harsh economic reality families faced by late summer. What makes the closing weeks of this campaign so compelling is the sheer, staggering scale of financial firepower being unleashed by the right. With over a billion dollars flooding the airwaves and a massive cash advantage held by Republican aligned groups, we are witnessing a desperate, high-stakes effort to defy political gravity through sheer advertising volume. Personally, I suspect this late messaging blitz will manage to salvage some seats, but it also raises a deeper question about what happens the morning after the election. Once the ballots are counted and the immediate drama of congressional control is settled, the political landscape will instantly pivot toward the 2028 succession race, forcing both parties to answer what they actually stand for, rather than just what they stand against.

highlights: Strait of Hormuz attacks surge as Iran steps up campaign against US-backed oil shipping | The National At least 12 tankers have been attacked in the strait in the past week, tally of UKMTO warnings shows At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, maritime agency reports show, as Iran increases its campaign to halt US-backed efforts to move oil through the vital waterway. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency issued delayed reports yesterday covering six vessels struck on Sunday – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage. The incidents follow a sustained increase in attacks, attempted attacks and the harassment of commercial vessels. The US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Centre said that showed Iran’s “intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels”. The centre's assessment followed reports of at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, quoting maritime security sources. Iran has accompanied the pressure on shipping with increasingly explicit warnings to vessels attempting to transit the strait. On Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a crude oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route with its navigation systems switched off. Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint co-ordinator of Iran’s army, issued a further warning on Sunday. “We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” he said. On Monday, the IRGC said it had struck a supertanker attempting to transit the strait with its transponders switched off. Seatrade reported a separate Iranian claim that a supertanker had been hit. The incident not been confirmed. Earlier this month, a crude tanker struck while trans of Hormuz, but extended beyond the waterway. A reported being hit by projectiles about 9 north of Madinat Ash Shamal in Qatar, with casualties reported. The attacks and warnings have sharpened the divide between Tehran’s claims of control over the waterway and Washington’s assessment of shipping conditions. Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the IRGC's commander, said Iran would close routes it considered to be illegal, including passages along Oman s coast. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected that assessment last week, saying commercial oil flows had largely recovered despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt shipping. “The Strait of Hormuz is open. There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he said. “So they’ve lost complete control of the strait.”

results.title: Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
highlights: Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts war on Iran stall | US-Israel war on Iran *IRGC warns against ignoring the ‘security and rules’ of the strategic waterway as US CENTCOM says it disabled vessel trying to run naval blockade.* **Tehran, Iran –** Strikes around the strategic Strait of Hormuz have picked up again as mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Saturday night that an unnamed crude oil supertanker hit a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route in the waterway with navigation systems turned off. In a statement, it warned of a similar fate for any oil tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime. On Sunday, a senior Iranian army official told state television that the country’s forces remain prepared for both defensive and offensive operations, more than seven months since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran on February 28. His comments came after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several incidents of military action or warnings against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman over the past day. It said ship masters in the vicinity of Ras al-Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), had been directed via radio broadcast overnight to move from their anchorages. And on Sunday afternoon, UKMTO reported ⁠an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker ⁠heading outbound through the Strait of ⁠Hormuz. Early on Sunday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) released footage of a fighter jet bombing the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and disabling its propulsion to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports. Since the US reimposed the blockade in mid-July, CENTCOM says its forces have disabled four commercial vessels, turned around 135 ships and destroyed 10 tankers linked with Iran. Washington says Tehran has exported no oil through the blockade line. This comes as at least a dozen ships were attacked over the week ending on October 5, the highest number since the war began. At least one was hit off the north coast of Qatar, signalling that the danger extends beyond the immediate Hormuz passage as Iran and the US vie for control. To reopen the strait and reach a resolution to the war, Iran has demanded a return to a now-collapsed memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June, as well as Washington’s backing of an already finalised Iran-Oman deal that designates temporary coordinated entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the strait. Messages continue to be exchanged between the two sides through mediators, although no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks leading to the US midterm vote, set to take place on November 3, and Israel’s election, due on October 27. US Vice President JD Vance said last week that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the war, signalling a potential easing of the oft-repeated US demand that zero enrichment must take place on Iranian soil. He also renewed criticism against the International Atomic Energy Agency for not condemning repeated US threats to again bomb Iran’s nuclear facilities.

results.title: Tehran raises the stakes, betting Washington will blink | Iran International
highlights: Despite signs of movement in negotiations with Washington, Tehran is showing little inclination to ease military pressure, pursuing diplomacy while signaling that renewed US attacks could trigger a broader regional response. The newspaper said Tehran had warned regional governments, publicly and privately, that renewed US attacks would prompt a wider Iranian response across the Middle East. The combination of diplomacy and military pressure reflects the central calculation facing Tehran: whether limited movement from Washington represents the beginning of a settlement or an attempt to weaken Iran's leverage without conceding its principal demands. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has said Washington accepted “some” of Tehran's seven conditions for de-escalation through Qatari and Omani mediators. But Iranian officials have characterized the US response as insufficient. At sea, there has been no corresponding easing of pressure. The Revolutionary Guards have continued to warn ships against using routes Tehran considers unauthorized, including alternative passages intended to circumvent Iranian restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Control over passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains one of Tehran's strongest sources of leverage. If US-protected shipping can routinely bypass Iranian restrictions, Tehran risks losing that leverage while continuing to suffer the effects of the US blockade on its own economy. Tehran's demands include an end to the blockade and the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. Allowing alternative routes to become normalized before securing substantial concessions would mean surrendering one of its most powerful bargaining tools. But maintaining that pressure is also hurting Iran. Its oil exports have effectively stopped under the blockade, with Kpler data showing no crude oil or condensate loaded onto tankers throughout September. Enforcing Iranian restrictions farther from traditional shipping lanes risks turning a struggle over the Strait of Hormuz into a broader confrontation involving neighboring states. Oman and Qatar have been central to mediation between Washington and Tehran. Any Iranian action threatening shipping close to Omani waters could complicate the diplomatic channel Tehran is simultaneously trying to preserve. Iran has not publicly announced plans to send forces across its borders, but the warnings appear designed to convince regional governments that another US campaign against Iran would not remain confined to Iranian territory. Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia have already demonstrated how quickly renewed fighting can spread beyond the direct US-Iran confrontation, threatening airports, energy infrastructure and regional shipping. For Tehran, that instability can increase pressure on Washington and its allies. But it also raises the possibility of an escalation Iran may struggle to control. Hardline and security-aligned voices portray Washington's willingness to engage with Tehran's proposals as evidence that military pressure has worked and argue Others favoring diplomacy see US movement as an opening that could disappear if attacks on shipping or neighboring states trigger another round of escalation. Gharibabadi captured that dual approach Tuesday, saying Iran had not shied away from diplomacy but was prepared for either outcome. For now, Tehran is pursuing both tracks simultaneously, negotiating while trying to demonstrate that failure to reach an agreement will remain costly — not only for Iran, but for the United States and its regional partners. The deterioration in most regional countries reflects renewed military exchanges and prolonged disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran faces the additional pressure of the US naval blockade. Iran's projected contraction nevertheless stands out, reflecting restrictions on its oil exports and an economy already weakened by years of sanctions and structural problems. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration would continue targeting those facilitating Iranian oil sales. Behnam Ben Taleblu, Iran Program director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, placed the subsequent airport attacks within Tehran’s broader efforts to recover regional influence. results.title: Iran's new strategy: Targeting oil shuttles to control the Strait of Hormuz - The Week
highlights: This new campaign of disruption is causing a severe shortage of available tankers and a massive spike in shipping costs, impacting global energy prices Ajish P Joy Published: October 13, 2026 01:05 PM IST Highlights - Iran is shifting its attacks to target the Gulf oil transport network, impacting southern transit corridors and anchorages off Oman - Recurrent attacks have caused a tanker shortage, driving freight costs up to 30 per cent of crude prices and forcing heavy discounts from Gulf producers - Iran has threatened US-linked digital and technology infrastructure in neighbouring states, including data centres and undersea cables, if the blockade continues Close encounter: Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman | Reuters As the transit of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz inches back up to normal levels, Iran seems to be reworking its strategy to stem the flow. Much of this flow is managed by an elaborate shuttle system operated by the Gulf states, especially the UAE, in close coordination with the US Navy. Smaller feeder vessels carry Gulf crude through a southern corridor near Oman and transfer it, ship to ship, onto Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) in the Gulf of Oman. Overland pipelines supplement the route. Together they have lifted exports from Arab producers to about 92 per cent of pre-war levels, even as the US naval blockade pushed Iran's own crude exports to zero in September. In response, Iran seems to be shifting its focus to the network that has allowed Gulf oil to bypass its grip. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claims to be hitting five to six ships a night, many of them outbound tankers operating with their transponders switched off. Mohsen Rezaei, the hawkish secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, has described the transfer system as a smuggling operation run by US Central Command and the UAE military. Tehran's response has been to widen the arc of its attacks. Drones and precision projectiles have reached southern transit corridors and anchorages off Oman, such as Sohar. By showing that vessels remain exposed even under Western naval cover, Iran hopes to persuade shipowners and insurers that the shuttle cannot guarantee safe passage. The IRGC Navy has cited mine threats, attributing recent tanker explosions to vessels transiting corridors without its clearance. Iran says the waterway is managed by a body it calls the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, and that commercial traffic must follow its directives. Iranian naval forces have also issued VHF radio instructions to vessels anchored off Ras al Khaimah in the UAE, asking them to leave immediately. The combination of physical hazard and administrative oversight is designed to present Iran as the sole gatekeeper of the passage. The economic effect may prove more telling than the strikes themselves. Recurrent attacks have left a shortage of tankers willing to transit the Gulf, and the shuttle is estimated to tie up 15 to 20 per cent of global VLCC capacity. Freight costs, which accounted for 1 to 3 per cent of crude prices before the war, have risen to 25 to 30 per cent. Gulf national oil companies have reportedly offered discounts of up to $35 a barrel below official selling prices to move cargo. Meanwhile, ship captains who are ready to make the trip are offered $100,000 a month, plus a $50,000 bonus for each trip. Iranian officials have said that if the blockade prevents Tehran from exporting, no other country in the region will be allowed to do so. Iran has also extended its warnings beyond shipping. Rezaei has cautioned that more than $2 trillion in US-linked technology assets in neighbouring states, including the UAE, could face retaliation if the blockade continues or foreign military action escalates. Data centres, artificial intelligence facilities, and undersea communications cables have been named. Digital infrastructure has already become a target in other theatres, with Ukraine repeatedly striking a Yandex data centre in Vladimir. For Gulf governments, the threat raises the cost of hosting American naval logistics. Washington remains the principal audience. Brent crude for December delivery stood at $103.33 a barrel yesterday, and prices above $100 present a political difficulty for any American administration ahead of midterm elections. Shortages of US air defence interceptors may add to the pressure, since escorting and protecting the shuttle depends on sustained supplies. Tehran has said it will not step back until Washington meets seven conditions, including the lifting of the naval blockade and the restoration of what it calls full maritime sovereignty. Proposals relayed through intermediaries are under review, but there is little sign of an early agreement. The strategy carries risks for Iran, but the alternatives are equally unappealing. Attacks on tankers could invite a stronger American response, and strikes near Omani anchorages may cost Tehran the goodwill of a state that has often served as a channel for dialogue. Gulf producers have already adapted once and could do so again, through added pipeline capacity, closer escorts, or transfer points beyond Iran's reach.

highlights: Iran is fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against the U.S. and its Gulf allies as it prepares for potential American attacks after the midterms and seeks to deter them. The government is also preparing Iranians for renewed war, sending paramilitary forces to read war stories to kindergartners, advertising training in firing shoulder-mounted antiaircraft missiles and holding rallies. Iran has little ability to defend against attacks from advanced U.S. jets, high-altitude bombers or cruise missiles, giving it an incentive to try to deter such attacks with threats. The belligerent tone also serves as a distraction from the deepening economic misery Iranians are experiencing as the U.S. toughens sanctions and pressures airlines not to fly to the country, tightening the blockade. In an attempt to deter a potential attack, some Iranian officials have hinted that their forces could conduct land incursions into neighboring countries, according to people familiar with the warnings. That would add to the threat Saudi Arabia faces from Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, who attacked its capital’s international airport over the weekend. A third aircraft carrier strike group and another Marine expeditionary unit are steaming toward the Middle East, and the Pentagon is weighing sending additional air-defense equipment and munitions to bases in the region, The Wall Street Journal has reported. While President Trump last week ruled out an attack before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, he has publicly mulled hitting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site, and U.S. officials have said that the military is preparing a range of options for new strikes. Instead, both are trying to break the logjam in their favor. The U.S. has ramped up its economic pressure campaign and is guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz with increasing success. At least three commercial vessels were hit over the weekend in and around the strait, according to U.K. Maritime Trade Operations, which is affiliated with the Royal Navy. Iranian officials are touting their efforts. The country’s airports, seaports and power plants “have prepared for wartime conditions,” installing shelters and backup supplies to continue operating in a crisis, Brig. Gen. Gholamreza Jalali, the official in charge of the country’s contingency plans, told reporters at the end of September. “In both word and deed, the Islamic Republic is actively preparing for the next war,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank. “In this sense the regime’s measures constitute both deterrence and war planning.”

highlights: Trump Rules Out Iran Strikes Until November as Hormuz Tankers Burn Tehran calls talks meaningless then offers revised terms, Washington says no strikes before the midterms while planning leaks, and the sea does the arguing. WASHINGTON — A tanker captain approaching the Strait of Hormuz this week is being told three different things by three different authorities. The Revolutionary Guards say the strait is closed. US Central Command says roughly 20 million barrels are still moving through it. And the maritime incident logs, which do not take sides, record tankers being hit. That contradiction is the story of the past fifteen days. After a United Nations week that produced a draft route toward a 60-day deal, the Iran war has settled into something harder to end than a battle: a bargain that neither Tehran nor Washington can afford to close, and neither can afford to walk away from. Two elections, Israel’s on October 27 and the American midterms on November 3, now sit over every decision, and officials on both sides insist they do not. The war began on February 28. A US naval blockade followed in April, a June memorandum eased it, and the ceasefire collapsed on July 8 after Iranian attacks on commercial ships in the strait, according to Wikipedia’s running chronology. Washington reimposed the blockade in mid-July. Everything since has been argued inside that frame. The last good news arrived in New York. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in talks mediated by Qatar, Pakistan and Egypt, and Iran floated a regionwide pause of up to 60 days with a phased reopening of Hormuz and an end to the blockade. Benjamin Netanyahu called the Iran ceasefire roadmap a trap on September 24, and Trump ruled out lifting the blockade first. Neither position has moved since. What moved instead was the sea. At least a dozen ships were attacked in the week ending October 5, the highest weekly count since the war began, Al Jazeera reported. UK maritime authorities logged five incidents on October 5 alone, four of them tanker attacks. On the same day Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the strait stays shut until seven conditions drawn from the June memorandum are met. The figures for how much oil is actually passing disagree sharply: the IMF’s PortWatch tracker counted just four transits on October 4 against a pre-crisis baseline of about 85 a day, while Kpler put crude flows for the week to October 7 at 8.5 million barrels a day, about 40 percent below normal, Al Jazeera reported. On October 6, President Masoud Pezeshkian declared negotiations with the United States “meaningless,” saying Iran had been attacked three times after earlier talks. He then said Tehran had revised its proposals and was ready to finalise them through the mediators, a reversal inside a single news cycle that tells you how little room anyone has to say yes out loud. What Iran wants is a return to the collapsed June memorandum and American backing for an Iran-Oman arrangement on temporary coordinated shipping routes. Washington’s messages have been harder to square. On October 8 Trump said the blockade “will remain in full force and effect” and that the United States would not strike Iran before the midterms, Axios reported. On October 9, at a rally, he told Iran it must “give us everything.” The same week, Israeli television reported US commanders had been told to prepare for a major attack within three weeks, and Israel’s military chief of staff reportedly warned that a strike could force a delay of Israel’s own election, the Times of Israel reported. Both things cannot be fully true. The only deadline on record came from Tehran, in the Iran Hormuz ultimatum its security chief gave Washington last month, and nothing in the past fifteen days suggests either capital is bound by one. The blockade itself is the clearest American instrument. Since mid-July CENTCOM says it has disabled four commercial vessels, turned back 135 ships and destroyed ten tankers it links to Iran, and Washington says Iran has exported no oil through the cordon. On October 11 a US fighter bombed the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to disable its propulsion, in footage CENTCOM released. Washington also sanctioned 17 more vessels in what it calls Iran’s shadow fleet, CBS News reported. And the sea fights back on its own terms. On October 10 the Guards said an unnamed supertanker hit a mine and burned after taking an unauthorised route with its tracking switched off, an IRGC tanker mine fire in the Strait of Hormuz that Eastern Herald reported with the caveat that the ship was unnamed and the account unverified. A day later the UAE coastguard rescued 22 crew from a burning tanker off its coast, cause unstated, and an unidentified projectile struck an outbound tanker in the strait. Oil is where the war touches everyone else. Brent traded between roughly $98 and $108 in the window, near $103 on October 10, against a 2026 peak above $126. Goldman Sachs estimates Gulf exports recovered to about 23.3 million barrels a day in September, though that includes cargoes moving with tracking off, and Saudi Arabia has restarted its East-West pipeline to bypass Hormuz. Saudi Aramco’s chief executive says inventories are thin and markets will stay under pressure until the strait fully reopens. Last month a Houthi strike sent the Brent crude oil price to $108.23 before an Iranian offer pulled it back. Hurricane Isaias then shut in Gulf Coast production on October 8, a second supply shock that had nothing to do with the war. Behind the shipping is the nuclear argument that never left. Vice President JD Vance says Iran must make a “meaningful” cut to its enrichment capacity. Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization spokesman Behrouz Kamalvandi says Tehran will pursue its interests through diplomacy if it can and “in the field of battle” if it cannot, and Iran says it may dilute high-enriched uranium in later talks but will not give up enrichment. Army chief Habibollah Sayyari says forces are ready for defensive and offensive operations. Putin has offered to help end the war, and Trump has talked up “productive discussions,” yet analysts quoted in the reporting see no sign that the core demands have moved closer. Trump and Iranian officials both say the midterms are not a factor in the talks, which is a claim neither side’s timetable obviously supports. What nobody has explained is the one question that decides the next fifteen days: whether the American planning leaks are leverage or intent. A president who says no strikes before November 3 and a Pentagon that has reportedly been asked for options cannot both be describing the same calendar. results.title: US prepares plans for new attacks on Iran - Gazeta Express
highlights: The US military is preparing options for resuming major combat operations against Iran, while President Donald Trump continues to show hesitation about returning to war, according to US officials. At Trump's behest, the Pentagon has drawn up plans for attacks on Iran's arsenal of drones and missiles, energy facilities and other military installations. However, Trump has repeatedly decided not to resume large-scale combat operations. The US military response to Iran has also been toned down in recent weeks, despite an increase in Iranian attacks on oil tankers. In a post on social media on Thursday, Trump declared that he would not attack Iran before the US midterm elections, saying that the two sides are holding "productive discussions", reports the Telegraph. According to officials, in recent months Trump's national security team and the Pentagon have presented him with five proposals for major operations against Iran or the Houthi rebels, backed by Tehran and based in Yemen. In each case, the president has rejected the plans. However, Trump has again called for the preparation of alternatives to attacks. Top national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed the plans last Friday at Camp David. According to people familiar with the proposal, they envision a short, intense campaign that would last about three days. The strikes would focus on Iran's missile and drone arsenal, much of which Iran's Revolutionary Guard has rebuilt since the early stages of the war. Potential targets would also include energy infrastructure, command centers, and Revolutionary Guard headquarters. The latest plans were previously reported by Axios. US officials have backed Trump's assessment that some progress has been made in diplomatic negotiations, which are being conducted through mediators. However, the talks remain deadlocked on the issue of Iran's nuclear program. Washington wants to first reach an agreement on Iran's nuclear ambitions, while Iranian negotiators insist that this issue be addressed at the end. In recent months, Iran has become a more formidable adversary, having improved its military tactics. More interceptors are now needed to intercept Iranian missiles than at the start of the war, putting pressure on America’s already stretched munitions stockpiles. Iran has also been using satellite imagery from Chinese companies to more precisely target American bases, according to people familiar with the intelligence reports. Since September, when the last significant exchange of retaliatory attacks took place, Iran has hit at least 13 ships, according to a monitoring group led by the British navy. Intelligence reports put the number higher at closer to 20, according to people familiar with the matter. None of these attacks has prompted a major US military response. Although oil exports from the Middle East have increased, increased Iranian attacks have worried shipping companies and raised questions the security of future energy shipments Over the summer, the U.S. military regularly responded to Iranian attacks on international shipping. The significantly more limited response recently reflects Trump's reluctance to resume full-scale warfare, officials said. American commanders are also concerned about the growing difficulty in stopping Iranian attacks on bases where American troops are stationed, as well as on energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in the region. In a tweet on Thursday, Trump insisted that none of the oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz comes from Iran. However, that claim has been questioned by people familiar with the intelligence reports. Iran allows passage to some ships that have paid fees or that may be carrying some of its oil. Iran also has its own secret tanker fleet, according to current and former officials. Chinese companies have paid tolls to pass through the strait, while Iran has long secretly blended its oil with Iraqi oil to evade sanctions. On Thursday, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on 17 ships it said were part of a secret fleet smuggling Iranian oil. Even some members of Trump's inner circle are increasingly expressing doubts that military action will change Iran's stance or plans. Some believe that the administration's campaign of economic pressure is working and that it just needs more time to force Tehran to make concrete concessions.
