Senior US officials worry that further operations could further deplete the global stockpile of defensive weapons needed to protect bases in the Middle East and intercept Iranian attacks. Other officials who support resuming operations argue that the Iranian economy continues to weaken and that a short but intense campaign could deepen Tehran's difficulties, especially if it harms its ability to control the Strait of Hormuz. The US continues to shoot down Iranian drones and cruise missiles, but has not attacked Iran's secret tanker fleet nor carried out retaliatory strikes inside Iranian territory. At the start of the war, the US military typically launched two interceptor missiles at approaching Iranian missiles, focusing on the most dangerous waves of attacks. Now, according to US officials, Iran's more advanced tactics and targeting have forced the US and its regional partners to use more missiles to stop attacks on US bases, euronews.al writes. US commanders say they still have a stockpile of interceptor missiles, although the war has depleted their stockpiles. US Central Command, which oversees military operations in Middle East, has also transferred weapons from Europe and Asia.

results.title: Trump Iran Strike Pledge: No Attack Before Midterms
highlights: President Donald Trump made a Trump Iran strike pledge late Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, saying the United States will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections because the two sides are holding “productive discussions.” Oil prices fell early Friday after the post, while Iran said it would answer a U.S. response to its Strait of Hormuz plan within days. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, according to Al Jazeera. The statement came after weeks of rising tension in the Gulf and speculation that renewed U.S. strikes could come before the vote. The pledge sets a time limit rather than an end to hostilities. The United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran on Feb. 28. A memorandum of understanding signed in June called for a halt to fighting on all fronts, but U.S. strikes resumed on July 8 after Washington accused Tehran of violating terms tied to the Strait of Hormuz. Trump’s post did not address what would happen after Election Day. Some analysts saw the timing as an effort to cool energy markets. Oil had climbed on Thursday on the possibility of new fighting, then eased once Trump ruled out an attack before the midterms, Al Jazeera reported. The U.S. buildup in the region, including a third aircraft carrier sent toward Iran, remains in place. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is reviewing the U.S. reply to Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and will respond “in the next few days,” with talks continuing through mediators, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported. Earlier this week, President Masoud Pezeshkian called negotiations with Washington “futile” and accused the United States of using talks as cover for attacks. The diplomatic signals have not calmed the waterway. Iranian media reported “massive explosions” in the southern Strait of Hormuz on Friday, with the Fars news agency citing unnamed military sources who said tankers using “unauthorized” routes may have hit sea mines. Moscow had earlier offered to mediate. Whether Iran’s coming reply to the U.S. proposal narrows the gap will shape the weeks left before the Nov. 3 vote. - Feb. 28: The United States and Israel launch military operations against Iran. - June: A memorandum of understanding calls for a halt to fighting on all fronts. - July 8: U.S. strikes resume after Washington accuses Tehran of violating terms tied to the Strait of Hormuz. - Monday, Oct. 5: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian calls negotiations with Washington “futile.” - Tuesday, Oct. 6: Vice President JD Vance says Iran must make a “meaningful” cut to its enrichment capacity. - Thursday, Oct. 8: Trump posts that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the midterms; Putin tells Pezeshkian Russia will “do everything” to help end the war. - Friday, Oct. 9: Oil prices ease; Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Iran will answer the U.S. reply within days. - Nov. 3: The U.S. midterm elections, the end of the window Trump described. Trump’s wording covers an attack “at any time prior to” Nov. 3, and he tied it to “productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.” It does not say what happens afterward, and it does not address the Hormuz incidents Iranian media describe, such as the reported mine strikes and nightly operations against vessels Tehran says break its rules. The practical test is whether Iran’s reply to the U.S. response narrows the gap on enrichment and Hormuz transit before the election.

results.title: Airstrikes Again: Why the U.S. and Iran Are Trapped in a Cycle of Retaliation - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights: ◆Washington Correspondent Lee Tae-kyu's Washington Playbook <210> Ahead of Midterms, Trump Wants Free Passage Through Hormuz Iran Won't Relinquish the Strait Before an Economic Aid Deal — a 'Fundamental Gap' Using Alternate Routes → Iranian Attacks → U.S. Airstrikes: A Vicious Cycle "The MOU Should Have Contained a Clear Agreement on Hormuz" "If the Current Situation Continues, a Return to All-Out War Is Possible" Attention is turning to the reasons why the United States and Iran are exchanging airstrikes despite signing a ceasefire memorandum of understanding (MOU) on the 17th of last month. Experts see it as stemming from a fundamental difference in positions between U.S. President Donald Trump, who wants free passage through Hormuz ahead of the midterm elections, and Iran, which does not want to lose its dominance over the Strait of Hormuz. They warn that the MOU should have contained a clear agreement on this issue, and that burying it was the source of trouble. If the current situation continues, they worry, the possibility of all-out war will grow. First, U.S. Central Command said on X (formerly Twitter) on the 8th that "at the direction of the U.S. commander-in-chief (President Donald Trump), it has launched additional airstrikes to degrade Iran's ability to threaten freedom of navigation in Hormuz." It marked the second consecutive day of airstrikes, following strikes on more than 80 targets the previous day. Reuters, citing a U.S. government official, reported that "the airstrikes on the 8th are expected to be larger in scale than those conducted the previous day." President Trump also posted photos of the airstrikes on Iran on Truth Social, writing, "This is retaliation for Iran's bombing of ships yesterday," and adding, "If this happens again, the situation will get much worse." Iran also signaled retaliation. Majid Mousavi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force, warned on X that Iran "will retaliate powerfully and swiftly." The United States carried out airstrikes for two consecutive days because Iran attacked merchant vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Between the night of the 6th and the morning of the 7th, Iran attacked three vessels, including a Qatari-flagged liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier, a Saudi-flagged oil tanker and a Liberian-flagged oil tanker. In response, the United States launched airstrikes on Iran on the 7th and revoked its sanctions waivers on Iranian crude oil. Iran, in turn, said on the 8th that it had struck 85 U.S. military facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait. On the 26th of last month, Iran also attacked merchant vessels, and the two sides exchanged attacks until the 28th, after which tensions eased following indirect talks brokered by a mediating country in Doha, Qatar. The Financial Times (FT) noted that "every time Iran attacks ships that do not use the Strait of Hormuz route it wants them to use, the United States attacks Iran, and Iran retaliates." There are a total of three routes through the Strait of Hormuz: one near Iranian territory proposed by Iran, one near Omani territory, and one through the passage between Iran and Oman. Iran is demanding that merchant vessels use only the route near its own territory, while the United States is encouraging vessels to use the route on the Oman side, escorting merchant ships from the air using fighter jets. One source told the FT that "with the emergence of the alternate route on the Oman side, Iran has lost control of the strait and is feeling frustrated." Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) told the FT, "Iran does not want to give up its influence over the Strait of Hormuz until a comprehensive economic aid agreement with the United States is reached," adding, "For President Trump, on the other hand, reopening the strait is the core of the MOU, and if it is not achieved, he will face enormous pressure from Republican hardliners to resume war with Iran." She warned, "Before signing the MOU, they should have reached a mutually acceptable agreement on the strait," and that "the longer the current situation continues, the greater the possibility that the United States and Iran will return to all-out war."

results.title: Iran IRGC Claims Third Tanker Hit in Two Days in Strait of Hormuz: Impacts on Consumers, Tanker Markets, and Investors - Energy News Beat
highlights: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday, October 12–13, 2026, that it struck a third “violating” or “offending” supertanker in the Strait of Hormuz within roughly 48 hours, sparking an onboard fire. The IRGC stated the vessel had switched off its navigation systems, ignored warnings, and attempted to exit via an unauthorized route, disrupting “order and security” in the waterway—the same pattern alleged in prior incidents involving mines or strikes. The claim, reported by Iranian state-linked outlets such as Press TV and covered internationally, has not been fully independently confirmed by bodies like the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) at the time of reporting. It fits a pattern of accelerated IRGC enforcement amid the ongoing US-Israel-Iran conflict that began earlier in 2026. Related incidents in the same period include drone and projectile strikes on other tankers (some involving Indian crew, with reports of missing seafarers on vessels such as the Nicaragua-flagged MT Petro Dolphin near Sohar anchorage), “dark” ships running with AIS off, and UKMTO advisories on multiple hits in and around the strait. IRGC statements have warned that cooperation with the US or use of unauthorized routes will draw a “decisive response,” and that enforcement may extend beyond the strait itself. The Strait of Hormuz remains a critical chokepoint. Flows have partially recovered from earlier wartime lows through a combination of risk-tolerant transits, ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, shuttling operations, and alternative routing/pipeline adjustments, but attacks continue to raise insurance, operational, and routing costs. What began as a crude supply disruption has evolved into a shipping crisis. Middle East flows rebounded sharply in September (reaching levels around 12 million barrels per day in some assessments after lower summer volumes), pulling a large share of the global VLCC fleet into the region. Analysts note that of roughly 923 VLCCs worldwide, hundreds are actively employed, with limited spare capacity once accounting for vessels tied up by blockades, sanctions-related restrictions, STS waiting times, and regional concentration. More than 40% of the VLCC fleet has been reported in or near the Persian Gulf/Gulf of Oman area at points, supported by shuttling and STS that can add days or weeks to voyages. The result is record or near-record freight rates. VLCC earnings on key Middle East–Asia routes have hit levels around or above $1 million per day (with peaks near $1.4 million in some reports), and assessed freight costs have soared: Middle East to China routes have been cited in the $24–35+/barrel range (versus single-digit dollars pre-war), while US Gulf to Asia fixtures have reached tens of millions of dollars per cargo (equating to $35–41+/barrel in some cases). All-in delivered costs for Asian buyers of Middle Eastern crude have been pushed into ranges that make alternatives from the Atlantic Basin or elsewhere more competitive on a landed basis in some analyses. Rates on non-Middle East routes have also tightened as the fleet is reallocated. Rebalancing is underway but expensive and incomplete. Key adjustments have included Chinese import moderation or stock draws at points, greater use of pipelines to outlets like Fujairah or Yanbu, and higher Atlantic Basin (including US and other Americas) exports. Yet persistent Hormuz risk, dark ship activity, and the concentration of vessels keep effective capacity tight and rates elevated relative to pre-conflict norms. As one analysis summarized the shift: earlier the issue was shortage of crude; now it is the high cost of moving it. US gasoline prices remain elevated. The national average for regular gasoline stood around $4.35 per gallon in mid-October 2026 (down modestly from recent peaks above $4.50 in May but still roughly $1.27 higher than a year earlier), according to AAA data. Prices are on track to break the 2022 record for the most days above $4 per gallon in a calendar year, per GasBuddy’s Patrick De Haan, and remain at record highs for this time of year in assessments from JPMorgan and others. Diesel has been even higher, around $6.25 per gallon nationally, directly feeding through to trucking, farming, and goods distribution. Geopolitical risk premiums in crude (Brent recently trading in the $104–106 range in mid-October data, with earlier spikes higher), refinery disruptions (including from Hurricane Isaias), and the elevated freight layer all contribute. Higher delivered crude costs and volatility support elevated product prices even as seasonal demand patterns and some inventory dynamics provide limited relief. For households, this sustains pressure on fuel budgets and broader inflation via transportation and goods costs. Further Hormuz incidents or sustained high freight would reinforce upside risks to pump prices heading into winter heating demand. - Shipping and tanker owners: VLCC and other crude tanker owners/operators are clear near-term beneficiaries of the rate spike and fleet tightness. High utilization, strong earnings, and potential for elevated rates into late 2026 or beyond (as long as Hormuz constraints and STS activity persist) are positive. Orderbook dynamics and any easing of regional concentration remain watchpoints. - Risks: Escalation that further disrupts flows, successful de-escalation that collapses the freight premium, demand destruction from sustained high prices, or inventory builds could reverse gains quickly. Insurance, war-risk, and operational costs remain elevated for participants in the trade. The IRGC’s latest claimed strike underscores that the Strait of Hormuz remains a live risk factor. For consumers, it reinforces the stickiness of high fuel prices. For investors, it highlights opportunities in the energy and shipping complex alongside the need for disciplined risk management as rebalancing continues at elevated cost.

results.title: Trump Rules Out Iran Strikes Before Midterm Elections — America Strikes
highlights: Trump said the US will not resume military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms, citing 'productive discussions,' as oil prices fell and new sanctions hit Iran's shadow fleet. President Trump said Thursday the United States will not resume military strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, a statement that sent oil prices lower and tempered weeks of speculation about an imminent resumption of combat operations. Trump made the declaration in a Truth Social post just after noon Eastern time, saying “we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” according to OilPrice.com. He added that his administration is having “productive discussions” with Tehran, a characterization reported by The Hill. The Associated Press confirmed the timeline, reporting that Trump explicitly tied the pause to the midterm calendar rather than to any broader ceasefire framework. The statement marks a shift from the administration’s posture just a day earlier. On Wednesday, the White House said Trump “has all options” on the table regarding Iran, with officials declining to rule in or out a resumption of strikes before the elections, according to The Hill. That ambiguity had kept oil traders on edge for much of the week. Thursday’s post removed that uncertainty, at least through November 3. Crude futures fell reversing some of the risk premium that had built up since the tanker attack off Qatar earlier this week, which pushed oil above $100 a barrel (see AmericaStrikes’ coverage). The military pause does not extend to economic pressure. The Treasury Department on Thursday imposed fresh sanctions targeting Iran’s “shadow fleet” — the network of tankers Tehran uses to move sanctioned oil while evading Western monitoring — according to Reuters. The move signals Washington intends to keep economic leverage on the table even as it steps back from military options ahead of the vote. Iran, for its part, has not softened its own posture in the region’s maritime chokepoints. Reuters reported this week that Tehran has vowed to block additional routes through the Strait of Hormuz, raising attack risks for commercial tankers even as the US-Iran military track cools, according to Reuters. That tension underscores that the Trump administration’s pledge covers US-initiated strikes on Iranian territory — not the broader risk environment across the Gulf, where Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and tanker incidents have continued this week (see AmericaStrikes’ reporting on the Riyadh airport closure). Analysts who track the oil market have said for weeks that the biggest near-term swing factor for crude prices is not Iran’s behavior but Washington’s. Trump’s post removes one major source of uncertainty for traders through early November, which is why the oil-price reaction was immediate even though nothing about the underlying regional risk — Houthi attacks, Hormuz threats, tanker strikes — has changed. The White House has not said what happens after the midterms. Trump’s own framing — that strikes are off the table “prior to” the election, not permanently — leaves open the possibility that military options return to active consideration once votes are counted. The administration has given no indication of what would trigger that reconsideration, or whether the “productive discussions” with Iran are aimed at a longer-term arrangement. For now, the practical effect is a six-week window in which the US has publicly committed to standing down on direct strikes against Iran, even as sanctions enforcement, Hormuz tensions, and the wider regional strike cycle — from Ukraine to the Red Sea — continue unabated.

results.title: Iran Has a Problem: The US Military Will Do Whatever It Takes to Blockade Iran and Cripple Tehran's Economy - National Security Journal
highlights: U.S. Fighter Jet Strikes Cargo Ship As Iran Blockade Intensifies – The U.S. military struck a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, October 10. Washington is stepping up efforts to prevent ships from entering or leaving Iranian ports and to show Tehran that, as its economy worsens, it won’t be able to force oil out of its ports, through the Strait of Hormuz, and into international waters. The operation comes as new evidence suggests that vessels continue to attempt to evade the American blockade, and as Iran intensifies its own attacks on commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The latest development comes only days after President Donald Trump announced that he would not launch new military strikes against Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. The latest operation, which saw an American fighter jet disable a Panama-flagged cargo vessel, suggests that even as Washington rules out a return to large-scale strikes, it will continue its existing maritime traffic enforcement campaign to Iran’s disadvantage. Meanwhile, new incidents reported on Sunday, October 11, suggest the conflict over commercial shipping is escalating, with Iran stepping up efforts to stop ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, even when under U.S. naval protection and traveling through U.S.-approved sea lanes. U.S. Central Command confirmed on Saturday that American forces struck the M/V Ocean Molica, which is also known as the Arika Sun, after its crew ignored repeated instructions to stop. The vessel had departed an Iranian port and was attempting to travel through the Gulf of Oman when American forces intervened. According to CENTCOM, a fighter jet fired a precision-guided weapon at the ship’s stern, destroying its ability to propel itself through the water. The military said no crew members were injured. It is the fourth time that American forces have disabled a commercial ship since the blockade resumed on July 14. The incident is part of a campaign to ensure that Iran cannot sell oil and generate revenue to support its strikes against commercial ships and energy infrastructure in neighboring countries, but it still attracted criticism from Democrats, including Senator Chris Murphy, who questioned the purpose of spending billions of dollars on military operations against commercial vessels. “What is this all for? Why are taxpayers paying billions to hit commericals [sic] ships? Apparently the goal is to gain leverage in order to convince the Iranians to let us pay them billions to return everything to the way it all was before the war. What a disaster,” Murphy asked on X. The strike may have been one of only a handful of actual military confrontations required to enforce the blockade, but many more ships have been turned around. According to a CENTCOM statement on October 10, U.S. forces have turned around 135 ships since July 14. highlights: agree to an 'energy ceasefire' : NPR **Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an 'energy ceasefire'** **President Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.** WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement. Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!" Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv. "Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening." The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia." In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. "We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ." On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal. Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. "Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made. The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure. He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. It authorises transactions in Russian-origin diesel, including imports into the United States, until 12:01 am Eastern time on 7 April 2027. The licence names no tonnage, buyer or price. The refinery-first design of the Trump energy ceasefire then asks Kyiv to pause the one campaign that has actually removed Russian diesel from the market. The IEA told AP that a refinery had been hit about every three days in recent months, a cycle of damage and emergency repair that can degrade units over time. Kpler analysts, cited by the Financial Times and relayed by Kyiv Post, put Russian refineries at about 60 per cent of installed capacity. These figures use different measures and should not be added together. ’s assessment, gap explains why the Trump energy ceasefire the easier ask to announce and the harder one to deliver. It targets a Ukrainian lever, while crude prices sits in the Gulf. TES In TES’s assessment, Moscow gains first. A pause in refinery strikes would let it repair units and move the volumes Trump has described, and the licence gives it a lawful buyer base. Under the Trump energy ceasefire, Kyiv loses its most effective long-range tool unless its own grid is protected in return. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure if Russia does the same, but a senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times, as relayed by Kyiv Post this week, that Kyiv would keep striking refineries despite the diesel deal. First, whether the Kremlin confirms the arrangement and states its scope. Second, whether Ukrainian refinery strikes pause and Russian diesel loadings begin, which ICE gasoil will register before any statement does. Third, whether Russian strikes on Ukraine’s grid stop, the exchange Kyiv has asked for. A fourth date sits further out: General License 135 lapses on 7 April 2027 unless Treasury renews it. Precedent is not encouraging. On 18 March 2025 Vladimir Putin ordered a 30-day pause on strikes against Ukrainian energy targets after a call with Trump. On 18 April 2025 the Kremlin said the month had expired, and both sides had accused each other of violations. Trump also announced an energy ceasefire in mid-September 2026, which neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed, Reuters reported via Investing.com. If Moscow accepts a refinery-only pause, the waiver and the truce become one transaction, fuel in exchange for restraint, with Kyiv as the party asked to pay. results.title: Trump's Diesel Deal with Putin Just Fractured the Western Alliance with Ukraine
highlights: A phone call between Trump and Putin produced a surprise Russian diesel deal — and pushed U.S.-Ukraine relations to the breaking point. Mateo Moreno / Published Oct 13 2026, 11:16 AM EDT The relationship between the United States and Ukraine has descended into its sharpest crisis since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, set in motion by a sequence of White House moves that Kyiv officials and international analysts are describing as a fundamental break from Western solidarity. The catalyst was a phone call, a Truth Social post, and the start of a very public unraveling. On October 9, President Trump announced he had personally arranged with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release over 4.8 million metric tons of Russian diesel into global markets — 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 more in November, and around a million tons shortly thereafter, with an additional 3 million to follow within a short period of time. To make the arrangement viable, the U.S. Treasury issued General License 135, temporarily waiving sanctions on Russian fuel exports through April 7, 2027 — unwinding years of coordinated economic pressure on Moscow. The political calculation was transparent: domestic diesel prices had passed $6 a gallon, and midterm elections are scheduled for November 3. The timing of the announcement struck Ukraine as a deliberate act of bad faith. Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were seated across from Ukrainian negotiators in Miami — alongside senior diplomats from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, the EU, and NATO — when the deal became public. Zelensky told Axios that his team learned of the arrangement barely an hour before Trump posted it, with no indication that any such agreement had been on the table. He described it as "not fair and not honest" and said it looked like "a happy birthday present for Putin" — a pointed reference to the Russian president's birthday earlier that week. He also argued that permitting Russian petroleum exports amounted to financing the very war effort his country is fighting to survive. The diesel arrangement did not emerge without a backstory. According to a U.S. official cited by CNN, Trump reached out to Putin after Ukraine disregarded at least half a dozen American requests to stop striking Russian oil refineries. A Reuters analysis found that Ukrainian forces had hit Russian energy infrastructure 58 times since August, a sharp acceleration from just three attacks in June and July combined. That sustained campaign is believed to have damaged roughly a fifth of Russia's overall refining capacity — a deliberate Ukrainian strategy to cut Moscow's war revenues at the source. The day after the deal became public, Trump made his frustration with Zelensky explicit. Speaking to reporters at the White House, he accused the Ukrainian president of repeatedly walking away from opportunities to end the war, then delivered a verdict that reverberated across diplomatic capitals: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," he said, adding that Kyiv needed someone who "knows how to negotiate." The statement was the most direct public assault on the legitimacy of an allied government that Washington has made since the conflict began. On October 11, Trump went further, posting on Truth Social that "there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," presenting the arrangement as an established fact. Ukraine had not been told about any such agreement. Within hours, Russian forces struck power plants in both Kharkiv and Kyiv — including the CHP-5 thermal plant in Kharkiv, hit at least twice, sparking fires — and a missile strike on a grocery store near Kharkiv killed three people and wounded nine, according to the Kyiv Independent. Zelensky answered the pressure with a response that was measured but pointed. In an interview on ABC's "This Week," he said it was "up to Ukrainians" to decide who leads the country, and noted that Putin, too, very much wants to change who governs Ukraine. He then issued a direct challenge to Washington: if the administration genuinely wanted elections, it should press Russia for a full 60-day ceasefire first. That condition carries legal weight — Ukraine's constitution prohibits holding elections under martial law, meaning any vote would require either lifting the state of emergency entirely or amending the constitution in the middle of an active war. Resistance arrived from Congress, where six senators — four Republicans and two Democrats — formally demanded the White House reverse its position on the diesel deal. The rebuke carried particular weight coming from members of Trump's own party, who had previously been anchors of the Russia sanctions framework. The administration gave no indication of reversing course. For Kyiv, the episode has accelerated a strategic reorientation that has been building since early 2025. Each Washington confrontation has, paradoxically, strengthened domestic Ukrainian support for Zelensky rather than weakening it. International analysts warn, however, that the pattern carries a growing cost: with the U.S. relationship now deeply strained, Ukraine faces a narrowing path toward any durable peace settlement — and toward securing the sustained backing it needs to negotiate from strength rather than desperation.

results.title: Trump says Russia and China aren't materially helping Iran, then admits he can't tell who to talk to anymore - The Monexus
highlights: Trump says Russia and China aren't materially helping Iran, then admits he can't tell who to talk to anymore In remarks carried on 13 October 2026, the US president said he doubts Moscow and Beijing are materially aiding Tehran, while OFAC moved new sanctions on alleged Iran-linked networks, and Trump conceded he can no longer identify a counterpart in Tehran. At 03:53 UTC on 13 October 2026, an Investing.com wire filed a single line: Donald Trump does not believe Russia and China are materially helping Iran. Over the next three hours the picture thickened. At 06:54 UTC, an OSINTLIVE relay of the Faytuks Network account noted the same news cycle included new OFAC designations against Iran-linked networks. At 07:02 UTC, Euronews' official Telegram channel carried Trump's longer version of the comment. By 07:26 UTC two more Trump statements were circulating: one captured by the Tsaplienko channel, one by Clash Report. Two claims were made in the same morning. The first: Moscow and Beijing are not, in any meaningful sense, sustaining Tehran. The second: Washington cannot identify an Iranian counterpart worth talking to. The two pieces do not obviously fit together, and that fit is the story. Trump's comments on the Russia-China-Iran link arrived in at least two registers. In what Tsaplienko's channel reports as a social-media post, he conceded a narrow possibility ("at a very low level") while denying the substantive one. To reporters, in the line carried by Euronews' Telegram, he went further, dismissing anyone who believed Russia and China were helping Iran as "an idiot and crazy." Tsaplienko's channel also relays what it characterises as the same remark in different wording ("morons and lunatics"), and reads those words as directed in part at members of the US intelligence services. That intelligence-services context is what the source material supplies; this article's assessment is that the choice of register is itself the signal. Each register does a different diplomatic job. The social-media post keeps the rhetorical door open to Moscow and Beijing, both of whom the White House is trying to manage on other files. The reporters' line sharpens that message into public ridicule of anyone who treats the three governments as a bloc. Whether that ridicule is aimed at hawks outside the administration, at named members of the intelligence services, or both, the available source items do not specify unambiguously, and this article cannot resolve it from the thread alone. The inconvenient sentence of the morning is the OFAC referral in the OSINTLIVE relay. OFAC designations require dossiers: directors of firms, vessels, shell-company maps. They are written on the working assumption that the enablers exist, are named, and can be hurt financially. The OSINTLIVE post says OFAC "recently issued" new sanctions targeting Iran-linked networks; it does not specify the calendar date of those designations, and the available source items do not say that the designations were issued on 13 October 2026. The dating matters. A Treasury acting weeks earlier than Trump's comments would describe policy momentum, not contradiction on a single day. A Treasury acting on the same morning would describe something closer to deliberate ambiguity at the top of the executive branch. This article cannot resolve which of those is true from the thread evidence. What the evidence does hold out, and what is therefore the most defensible reading, is that the president publicly downplayed the role of Russia and China while his own sanctions enforcement apparatus continued to act on the contrary working assumption. The 07:26 UTC remarks add a separate pressure. Clash Report carries Trump saying the United States "might have gone too far" with Iran's leaders and that officials no longer know who they are dealing with. If read literally, that is an admission that years of maximum pressure have not produced a recognisable negotiating partner. If read as rhetoric, it is the kind of line written when an administration wants to reset its own framing of why talks are not happening. Either reading lands on the same operational problem. Without a counterpart, the Treasury's file-by-file approach becomes the de facto policy, in lieu of diplomacy. The Iran brief is being run, in effect, from OFAC rather than from the negotiating table. Monexus assessment: that arrangement is consistent with what the thread documents, but is a structural inference from the evidence, not a quote. Three things remain unsettled by the available material. The dating of the OFAC designations: "recently" is not the same as "today," and the wire evidence reviewed here does not let this article close that gap. The wording of Trump's reporters-remark: "idiot and crazy" per Euronews' Telegram against "morons and lunatics" per Tsaplienko, with the second channel reading some or all of the line as aimed at his own intelligence services. And the venue: which Trump statements came from a social-media post and which came in person to reporters is implied by Tsaplienko and Euronews respectively, but the source items do not specify the platform or location in unambiguous terms, so this article treats the venue split as the channels' framing, not as an established fact. The most natural reading of the thread is that Trump is running a useful ambiguity. Downplaying the Russia-China link keeps the door open to Moscow and Beijing on their separate files. Admitting he cannot identify an Iranian counterpart pre-empts criticism when talks fail to materialise. The sanctions move regardless. That is the documented shape of the morning; whether it constitutes a policy or a posture is exactly what the contradictions will not let a reader resolve.
